item.title: Korea Times holds first Global Supporters reunion
item.description: The Korea Times held its first Global Supporters Homecoming Day on Friday, bringing together 60 former and current honorary ambassadors of the English-language daily from 35 countries, with the theme “Once a supporter, always family.” The inaugural event brought together members of three recent cohorts. It was a festive reunion for international students and expats in Korea who have served as ambassadors for the newspaper during a six-month term. Participants could network across cohorts and academic backgrounds, taking part in recreational activities with gift offerings. Organizers said the event was meant to keep supporters connected after their terms end, gathering alumni and current members in one place for the first time. “Although we are from different cohorts, it feels special that we are all here together with the same wish to share Korea’s stories with the world,” said Anna Scierska from Poland, representative of the latest cohort. “I hope that, regardless of cohort, we can keep in closer touch and get along well with each other.” Scierska said her participation in

item.title: Belgian authorities force Google to halt data center construction
item.description: BRUSSELS, Belgium — Belgian authorities have ordered Google to suspend construction of a data center in the south of the country because of a lack of proper planning permission, a regional official said Friday. "We have identified a major offense: the illegal construction of a building covering three hectares," or 7.4 acres, Nicolas Yernaux, spokesman for the Wallonia regional authorities, told AFP. The "stop-work" order at the former mining site covering some 50 hectares in total comes after NGO Greenpeace accused Google of carrying on construction despite lacking the correct permits. The regional authority said that inspectors visited the site on Thursday to inform Google representatives to halt construction. The mammoth project has been locked in legal litigation for months after Google applied to amend the terms of its planning permission. The application sought to allow a cooling system for the facilities using water drawn from the nearby River Sambre, whereas the initial project had envisaged air cooling, Belgian media reported. item.title: US chip restrictions cast shadow over Chinese AI labs
item.description: BEIJING — Chinese AI labs like Z.ai, DeepSeek and Moonshot AI have been creeping ever closer to their U.S. rivals in their capabilities, but the fallout from the Nvidia scandal could slow their progress. Experts said tighter U.S. restrictions are curbing access to chips in the short term, which adds incentive for Beijing's efforts to accelerate development of their own cutting-edge semiconductors. How is Washington cracking down? The U.S. government first introduced export controls on advanced chips destined for China in 2022, citing national security concerns as the two countries race to develop powerful AI technology. The following year, Washington tightened its rules to stop Chinese AI companies using overseas affiliates to place orders for high-end chips made by U.S. industry leader Nvidia. Many Chinese players then turned to renting cloud computing power from data centers located overseas, especially in Southeast Asia. item.title: UN warns hunger will deepen in Middle East as war, fuel costs, aid cuts collide
item.description: CAIRO — Hunger is expected to worsen in 16 countries over the next six months, with war-torn Sudan and Yemen among five nations facing the gravest risk, the United Nations’ food agencies warned Friday. The agencies pointed to conflict, soaring fuel costs linked to war in the Middle East and steep cuts in aid. The Food and Agriculture Organization and the World Food Program's Hunger Hotspots report covers December through May 2026. It places Sudan, Yemen, South Sudan, Somalia and northern Nigeria at the highest level of concern. All five have appeared on the list repeatedly since 2022. The Palestinian territories were moved down one level following the October 2025 ceasefire in Gaza, though 67 percent of Gaza’s population still faces crisis-level hunger or worse, and the report warned that the gains were fragile. Famine risk persists in Sudan In Sudan, a risk of famine is expected to persist through January in 13 areas of North Darfur and South Kordofan, the report said. item.title: Kakao founder's acquittal finalized as prosecutors decide not to appeal
item.description: Prosecutors have decided not to appeal an appellate court's acquittal of Kim Beom-su, founder of tech giant Kakao Corp., of stock manipulation charges, making the not-guilty verdict final, Yonhap News Agency learned Friday. Last week, the Seoul High Court acquitted Kim, indicted on charges of violating the Capital Market Act in connection with Kakao's 2023 takeover of K-pop agency SM Entertainment, upholding a lower court's ruling. Friday was the deadline to appeal, but the Seoul Southern District Prosecutors Office said it had decided not to challenge the ruling following a review of both the first-instance and appellate court decisions. The Kakao founder was accused of making large-scale purchases of SM Entertainment shares to push their price above rival Hybe's tender offer price, thereby blocking Hybe's takeover of SM. In October last year, the Seoul Southern District Court acquitted him, ruling that the fact that Kakao's large-scale purchases of SM shares affected their price did not necessarily constitute price manipulation. item.title: 'YOMO JOMO': Seulgi Lee's playful, many-sided look at everyday objects
item.description: What do you see when you look at an everyday object from every angle — or, in Korean, "yomo jomo"? Seulgi Lee, a Paris-based artist who turns Korean proverbs, folk songs and artisans’ techniques into playful sculptures, installations and sound works, poses that question in her first solo show at a public art museum in Korea. “YOMO JOMO Seulgi Lee” opened Thursday at the Seoul Museum of Art's (SeMA) main Seosomun branch and runs through Feb. 28. Lee, born in 1972, has lived in France since 1992 and was selected the 2020 Korea Artist Prize winner. The show brings together more than 70 works, including nine new pieces commissioned by SeMA and serial projects dating to the late 1990s. Lee names her shows around the world in Korean, drawn to the language’s onomatopoeia and mimetic words, which often repeat a syllable in a playful rhythm. This year’s Bordeaux show, “GORU GORU,” uses a word meaning “evenly” or “equally.” It echoes the name of the Garonne River, which flows through the city, and Lee said its rounded sound reminded her of water gurgling along. item.title: Yonsei University unveils $97.4 mil. plan for human-centered AI campus
item.description: Yonsei University will invest more than 130 billion won ($97.4 million) over eight years to bring artificial intelligence (AI) into its education, research and administration, the school said Friday. At a ceremony on its Sinchon campus, President Yoon Dong-sup unveiled "Truth that Frees, Intelligence that Serves" as the university's vision for the AI era. The slogan draws on Yonsei's founding motto, "The truth will set you free." "Knowledge can be acquired anywhere, but it is only on campus that people can come together, communicate, exercise judgment collectively and take responsibility," Yoon said. The university said the vision means training students to question, check and look for the truth themselves instead of passively accepting AI-generated answers, and to use what they learn to serve others and society. Starting with the 2027 academic year, Yonsei will offer a general education course titled "Artificial Intelligence and Contemporary Society." item.title: Shin Min-a says she would return for 'The Remarried Empress' Season 2
item.description: Actor Shin Min-a, who played Empress Navier in the Disney+ romantic fantasy hit "The Remarried Empress," said Friday she hopes to return for a second season should it be made. Featuring a star-studded cast that also includes Ju Ji-hoon, Lee Jong-suk and Lee Se-young, the Korean original series follows Empress Navier and her husband, Sovieshu (Ju), whose seemingly peaceful marriage is upended by the arrival of Rashta (Lee Se-young), a former runaway slave. The series, based on a Korean web novel of the same name, which has also been made into a webtoon and racked up billions of views, drew attention as a live-action adaptation of a romantic fantasy story. "It was a long journey that concluded well thanks to the many people who supported the character," Shin told reporters in a group interview. "When I read the script, I felt that a second season should follow ... I hope there is a second season and they will need me (as Navier)," she said playfully. item.title: Illit's Moka announces return after 5-month health hiatus
item.description: Moka of K-pop girl group Illit is set to gradually resume activities after taking a five-month hiatus due to health concerns, paving the way for the group's long-awaited reunion as a five-member act. On Friday, the Japanese member shared the news through the fan community platform Weverse, expressing gratitude to fans who had waited for her return. "First of all, thank you so, so much to all the GLLITs who have been waiting for me. Thanks to the fans who waited for me and everyone who helped me, I'm able to greet you like this once again," Moka said, referring to the group's official fandom. "I'm really happy, too, and I feel like I've been waiting for this day all along. I'll do my best to gradually resume activities with the members, so I hope you'll be patient with me." She also expressed her affection for fans. "I hope GLLITs are always happy and surrounded by good things," she said. "I'm always grateful, and I love you." item.title: Pan-gov't task force on integration of military academies to set sail next week
item.description: The defense ministry said Friday it will launch a pan-government task force to push ahead with its plan to establish a unified military academy of the Army, Navy and Air Force for joint education and training in the central city of Daejeon. The task force, comprising some 20 personnel from the military, education and land ministries, will launch for operation Wednesday to follow through on plans to merge the military academies of each armed service. The ministry announced last week a finalized plan to establish a single military academy while retaining the existing school of each armed service as regional campuses, amid fierce pushback from alumni groups and cadets over the plan. The task force will focus on overhauling the education system to ensure the envisioned military academy can nurture elite officers to lead future warfare, the ministry said. Meanwhile, the ministry disclosed the results of a survey conducted on 2,526 military cadets from Nov. 13-17 over their opinions of the integration blueprint. item.title: Parliamentary committee adopts confirmation hearing report for justice minister nominee
item.description: A parliamentary committee on Friday adopted a confirmation hearing report for Justice Minister nominee Lee Yong-cheol, paving the way for his appointment. The report was adopted at a meeting of the legislation and judiciary committee led by the ruling Democratic Party of Korea (DPK), with the main opposition People Power Party (PPP) leaving the session in protest of the move. The PPP has criticized the nominee over suspicions that he could seek to drop indictments against President Lee Jae Myung. The DPK-dominated National Assembly earlier passed a special counsel bill to launch a probe into allegations that prosecutors under the previous administration had indicted Lee and others on fabricated evidence. The PPP suspects the nominee could order the prosecution to drop the indictments based on the results of the probe. The president faces several trials on various charges, including those on his alleged involvement in corrupt development schemes and illegal remittances to North Korea stemming from his time as mayor of Seongnam and governor of Gyeonggi Province. item.title: Prosecutors demand dismissal of Daejang-dong scandal suspects' appeals
item.description: Prosecutors on Friday asked an appellate court to dismiss appeals filed by five key figures in a development corruption scandal linked to President Lee Jae Myung, who were sentenced to prison terms last year. Prosecutors made the request during a hearing at the Seoul High Court, where the five defendants stood trial over their roles in the Daejang-dong development scandal that occurred in Seongnam, just south of Seoul, in 2015, when Lee was the city's mayor. The scandal centers on allegations that a small number of obscure private asset management firms, including Hwacheon Daeyu, were allowed to reap astronomical profits from the project. In October last year, the Seoul Central District Court sentenced Yoo Dong-gyu, former acting president of Seongnam Development Corp., and Kim Man-bae, major shareholder of Hwacheon Daeyu, to eight years in prison each on charges including breach of duty. Kim was also ordered to forfeit 42.8 billion won (about $32 million). Two lawyers and an accountant involved in the case received prison terms ranging from four to six years. All five defendants appeal

item.title: Busan seeks path to inclusive city as foreign population grows
item.description: As Busan's international community continues to grow, the southeastern port city is looking beyond attracting foreign residents to a bigger challenge: making sure they can fully participate in everyday life and feel that they belong. Busan Metropolitan City held its 2026 Busan Inclusive City Forum on Friday at Busan City Hotel, bringing together foreign residents, Korean citizens, academics and public officials to discuss ways to build a more inclusive community. The gathering comes as the city's population becomes increasingly diverse. According to figures from the Ministry of the Interior and Safety, Busan had 88,542 foreign residents in 2024, up from 73,185 in 2020 — an increase of about 21 percent. Foreign residents accounted for 2.7 percent of the city's total population in 2024. The figures include not only foreign nationals but also naturalized citizens and children from multicultural families, reflecting the increasingly diverse makeup of communities across the city. item.title: Pioneering educator Trudy Kim, wife of FEBC-Korea chairman, dies at 88
item.description: Trudy Kim, a pioneering educator and the wife of Rev. Billy Kim, chairman of the Far East Broadcasting Company (FEBC)-Korea, died early Friday. She was 88. Born in Michigan in 1938 as the third of four children, she met Billy Kim while studying education at Bob Jones University, where he was an international student from Korea. The couple married in 1958 and moved to Korea the following year, when the country was still recovering from the 1950-53 Korean War. She spent 67 years in Korea, saying she regarded it as her second home. In 1978, Kim founded Central Christian Kindergarten in Suwon and served as its principal for 39 years until retiring in 2017. She laid the foundation for inclusive education, in which children with and without disabilities learn together, at a time when the idea was still unfamiliar in Korea. Kim donated her entire salary to the kindergarten. Instead of staying in the principal’s office, she cleaned the restrooms herself. item.title: Defense minister visits Army's drone testing unit amid push for unmanned systems
item.description: Defense Minister Kang Shin-chul on Friday visited an Army mobilization unit operating drone pilot programs, the defense ministry said, as the military pushes to reshape its reserve forces into an unmanned systems-centered force amid a demographic change. Kang paid a visit to the 72nd Infantry Division, a reserve force mobilization unit north of Seoul, earlier in the day, to inspect its drone testing and meet with service members and reserve forces there, the ministry said in a release. The 72nd Infantry Division has been running a drone and robot company under its wing as part of an Army initiative to transform reserve force units into drone-centered ones. Speaking to the troops at the unit, Kang called on active-duty soldiers and reservists to grow together as "one warrior community armed with professional expertise and combat readiness," vowing to build a "strong military" that prevails against any threat. item.title: KOSPI surges over 4%, Kosdaq gains top 8% on hopes for market stabilization fund
item.description: The benchmark KOSPI surged more than 4 percent Friday, as expectations for government measures to stabilize the stock market, including the possible deployment of a market stabilization fund, lifted investor sentiment. The tech-heavy Kosdaq index also jumped more than 8 percent to reclaim the 700 mark for the first time in 12 trading sessions. KOSPI closed at 4,915.68, up 4.34 percent from the previous session. The index opened at 4,728.80 and fluctuated during the morning session before extending its rally in the afternoon. Heavy net buying by foreign investors drove the index sharply higher, with institutional purchases adding to the gains. item.title: Korea to tighten visa checks on foreign entertainers to curb trafficking
item.description: Korea plans to tighten visa screening and workplace inspections for foreign entertainers to prevent human trafficking, including sexual exploitation and forced labor. The Ministry of Gender Equality and Family convened an interagency policy coordination meeting on human trafficking prevention on Friday, focusing on strengthening protections for foreign nationals entering the country on E-6-2 entertainment visas. The visa allows foreign nationals to work as singers, musicians and other performers at hotels and entertainment establishments. However, some have been subjected to sexual exploitation and forced labor after entering the country under the pretext of pursuing entertainment careers. The ministry discussed ways to strengthen information sharing among relevant agencies during the performance approval and visa screening processes to identify potential trafficking risks before foreign entertainers enter Korea. Discussions also focused on tightening oversight of entertainment agencies and workplaces through joint inspections and stronger follow-up measures against violations. Other propo

item.title: [COVER STORY] Migrant groups hope ruling on political activities will give foreign residents stronger voice
item.description: Migrant support groups expressed hope Friday that the Constitutional Court’s landmark ruling against a blanket ban on foreign residents’ political activities will give residents greater freedom to speak out on issues that directly affect their lives. In a 6-3 decision Thursday, the court found the Immigration Act provision unconstitutional, 49 years after it was introduced. The court said the ban violated the principle of proportionality by restricting foreign residents’ freedom of expression more than necessary. For years, the broad restriction on political activities has left foreign nationals uncertain about where the line falls between legitimate advocacy and prohibited activity, according to Udaya Rai, head of the Migrants' Trade Union. "Immigration authorities have interpreted the provision too broadly. We have long feared visa-related disadvantages because even speaking at a rally organized by a political party or taking part in a public forum could be interpreted as political activity," Rai said. item.title: KGC targets healthy aging market with premium deer antler products
item.description: As healthy aging gains importance, consumers are showing renewed interest in traditional health ingredients such as red ginseng and deer antler. They are becoming more selective about their purchases, paying closer attention to ingredient quality, manufacturing processes and brand credibility. Health supplement maker KGC is tapping into this trend with Cheon Nok, its premium deer antler brand under Jung Kwan Jang, as it seeks to differentiate its products through ingredient quality and manufacturing expertise. The brand uses deer antlers sourced from New Zealand as its main ingredient, combined with traditional ingredients such as red ginseng, and applies systematic quality controls throughout the process, from raw material selection to manufacturing. The company said the deer antler used for the brand carries the Super A Traditional grade, which it describes as the highest grade guaranteed by the New Zealand government. Deer antlers are graded according to several criteria, including thickness, length and weight, with the company sourcing raw materials that meet the strictest standards.

item.title: Jin Air's Busan relocation complicates workforce integration
item.description: Jin Air’s decision to base its postmerger headquarters in the southern port city of Busan has reignited questions over whether the airline can relocate its key personnel and management functions, with opposition from employees and labor unions threatening to complicate the transition, experts and industry officials said Friday. Starting March 17 next year, the integrated Jin Air is set to officially begin its operations following its merger with Air Seoul and Air Busan. The relocation of integrated Jin Air’s headquarters to Busan came after the local community, which stands to lose Air Busan as a key regional carrier following the merger, repeatedly opposed the plan and strongly pressed for the new airline’s headquarters to be based in the city. item.title: US Apache squadron's inactivation raises questions over combat readiness in Korea
item.description: Analysts are questioning whether U.S. combat capability in South Korea has been diminished after U.S. Forces Korea (USFK) confirmed the inactivation of an Apache helicopter squadron at Camp Humphreys, with no replacement unit yet in place. USFK said Thursday that the move did not affect the allies' military readiness or ability to deter an attack, but the command did not say whether the squadron's helicopters and personnel had been reassigned within South Korea or moved out of the country. Shin Jong-woo, secretary general of the Korea Defense and Security Forum, questioned whether the U.S. could maintain the same capabilities on the peninsula after taking an aviation unit out of service before a replacement was in place. He said no additional unmanned aircraft had been deployed to take over the squadron’s duties and that U.S. combat capability on the peninsula could suffer even if troop numbers stayed the same. “As a rule, you bring in a replacement before you take an existing unit out of service,” Shin said. item.title: Why Xi's warning against a 'blind' tech rush is suddenly ringing louder
item.description: Chinese President Xi Jinping's warning last month against a disorderly rush into new industries has come into sharper focus this week with an investigation into Shanghai's party chief, a sell-off in chip stocks and renewed questions about whether China's computing boom can pay for itself. During an October 16 visit to Ulanqab, a computing hub in north China's Inner Mongolia autonomous region, Xi cautioned against blind competition and development that ignored local conditions. Then on Wednesday, Study Times, an official publication run by the Central Party School, invoked Xi's remarks in a commentary piece warning that some localities had rushed to secure land and resources and bought chips without adequately assessing customers' needs. The commentary appeared a day after authorities announced that Shanghai party secretary Chen Jining was under investigation for suspected serious violations of discipline and law. item.title: Ex-gymnast Son Yeon-jae, husband pledge $2.23 mil. to support high-risk pregnancies
item.description: Former rhythmic gymnast Son Yeon-jae and her husband, Lee Jun-hyo, have pledged 3 billion won ($2.23 million) to the Yonsei University Health System to support mothers experiencing high-risk pregnancies and their babies. Severance Hospital said Friday that the couple signed a donation agreement with the Yonsei University Health System to establish and operate the Yeon-jae Fetal Care Center. The center will provide comprehensive medical services for women with high-risk pregnancies and their babies, covering everything from pregnancy and childbirth to postnatal treatment. Specialists in obstetrics, neonatology and other relevant medical fields will work together to assess the health of mothers and their unborn babies and respond promptly to potential complications before and after delivery. The center will also establish a remote consultation system connecting medical institutions in Korea and overseas through high-resolution diagnostic equipment and real-time information-sharing technology. item.title: Chinese envoy warns US-Korea alliance shouldn't become 'tool' against China
item.description: Chinese Ambassador to Korea Dai Bing said Thursday that the Korea-United States alliance should not become a constraint on bilateral relations between Seoul and Beijing, voicing concerns over Washington's push to modernize the alliance and expand the strategic flexibility of U.S. Forces Korea (USFK). "Any country should maintain its autonomy. We respect the Korea-U.S. alliance, which has a long history," Dai said at a press conference in central Seoul, a week after China hosted the 2026 Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit in Shenzhen. He said China never asked Korea to choose between Washington and Beijing, adding that he believed Seoul has the wisdom to develop relations with both. However, he questioned the implications of Washington's push to modernize the Korea-U.S. alliance and expand its strategic role. "Terms such as 'modernization of the Korea-U.S. alliance' and 'strategic flexibility' carry, to some extent, an implication of targeting China," the ambassador said. item.title: DPK lawmaker handed 'severe' disciplinary action over remarks on Lee
item.description: The ruling Democratic Party of Korea (DPK)'s ethics committee on Friday decided to suspend Rep. Choi Min-hee, a member of its Supreme Council, from party membership for two years over her controversial remarks about President Lee Jae Myung, sources said. If the punishment is finalized, Choi will be ineligible to run in the 2028 general elections. Choi recently came under fire for her remarks suggesting that Lee, when he was the party's leader, had opposed former President Yoon Suk Yeol's impeachment, and for referring to journalists as "a pack of hyenas." Choi's case was referred to the party's ethics committee after DPK leader Kim Min-seok ordered an internal inspection earlier this month. "We determined that some of Supreme Council member Choi's remarks, which were problematic, damaged the party's dignity and decided to take severe disciplinary action after comprehensively reviewing various circumstances," Lee Chang-hwan, head of the ethics panel, told reporters. item.title: Lee's pick to lead capital market reform faces tests on shareholder rights, Kosdaq overhaul
item.description: Meritz Financial Group Vice Chairman Kim Yong-beom, President Lee Jae Myung’s pick to lead a new capital market reform committee, will be tasked with strengthening protections for minority shareholders and overhauling the Kosdaq market, industry officials said Friday. Kim, who reshaped Meritz’s corporate structure and expanded shareholder payouts, will now have to persuade policymakers to act on proposals from private sector experts. The Financial Services Commission (FSC) said its chairman, Lee Eog-weon, met with Kim at Government Complex Seoul on Thursday to discuss the committee’s composition and remit. The meeting followed the president’s call at a Nov. 13 policy meeting for a high-level body to lead capital market reform. “Kim has already put into practice the changes the government is seeking to promote through policy, such as enhancing shareholder value and strengthening investor relations,” the FSC chairman said. “He will draw on his experience in business and the markets to set the reform agenda and serve as a bridge between the government and market participants.

item.title: 'Who is our main enemy?' South Korea's Gen Z weighs in
item.description: "Who is South Korea's main enemy?" For many young South Koreans, the answer may be North Korea, but being asked the question itself can feel like a test of their political beliefs. In a roundtable discussion organized by the Hankook Ilbo, participants in their 20s revealed nuanced attitudes toward national security, Korean reunification and North Korean defectors. While many identified North Korea as the country's main enemy, some questioned why individuals should be required to publicly affirm that position. Opinions were also divided over the need for reunification, although participants broadly agreed that North Korean defectors deserve support from South Korean society. item.title: Seoul turns to AI to spot falling concrete risks on bridges, overpasses
item.description: Seoul is turning to artificial intelligence (AI) to tackle a potentially deadly hazard on its bridges, developing a new inspection system that can detect concrete at risk of breaking loose without requiring workers to climb beneath structures. The Seoul Facilities Corporation said Thursday it had jointly developed an AI-powered diagnostic device with a private company to identify the risk of concrete spalling, in which pieces of concrete detach and fall from bridge structures. The technology was recently recognized as an outstanding case in the Ministry of the Interior and Safety's collection of successful public sector AI and advanced technology projects. Until now, inspections of bridge decks have largely relied on workers riding elevated inspection vehicles and striking concrete surfaces with hammers, then judging the condition of the structure by listening to the resulting sounds. The approach has created several challenges, including lane closures, traffic congestion, inspection costs, safety risks associated with working at height and inconsistent assessments depending on workers

item.title: Singapore 'engaging' with local firms over US chip restrictions
item.description: SINGAPORE — Singapore said Friday it was "engaging" with local businesses over tightened U.S. export controls on advanced AI chips designed by tech titan Nvidia. But Deputy Prime Minister Gan Kim Yong said he was unable to confirm reports that the U.S. firm had halted server shipments to four Southeast Asian countries. Citing national security concerns, the United States has since 2022 restricted exports to China of Nvidia's industry-leading chips, which are used to train and run AI tools. Washington last week moved to close a loophole in those controls in the wake of a scandal that has engulfed Nvidia, forcing out longtime CEO Jensen Huang before his reinstatement on Sunday. The new U.S. rules crack down on alleged chip smuggling to China, as well as the large grey market of Chinese companies renting computing power from data centres in third countries, often in Southeast Asia. "We are in the process of engaging our businesses, to reach out to them to see how this impacts their businesses," Gan told a local summit in Singapore on Friday. item.title: Chinese military tests new Taiwan landing tactics in coastal drills
item.description: TAIPEI/HONG KONG — China is staging a weeks-long amphibious landing drill in the province facing Taiwan, testing a new method to land troops ashore by linking civilian vessels into a makeshift floating bridge, satellite images and a research report showed. China views democratically governed Taiwan as its own territory, despite Taipei's rejection of Beijing's sovereignty claims, and has never renounced the use of force to bring it under Chinese control. The exercise, in Dacheng Bay in China's southeastern province of Fujian, was first spotted on November 1, according to satellite images and a report by geospatial data company ingeniSPACE reviewed by Reuters. "The People's Liberation Army appeared to be rehearsing low-signature methods to provide logistical support to forces that could be involved in a first island chain invasion scenario," said Jason Wang, the company's chief operating officer. item.title: Kumho Mitsui Chemicals wins award for sustainability report
item.description: Kumho Mitsui Chemicals has won an award for its sustainability report at the 2026 Korea Sustainability Conference, earning recognition for its efforts to improve transparency in environmental, social and governance disclosures and advance resource recycling in its manufacturing operations. Kumho Petrochemical Group’s chemical manufacturing arm said that its 2026 sustainability report was selected as an outstanding report in the manufacturing category of the Korean Readers’ Choice Awards. Organized by the Korean Standards Association, the awards recognize corporate sustainability reports based on global reporting initiative guidelines and evaluations by stakeholders and experts. The latest report is Kumho Mitsui Chemicals' fourth since it began voluntarily publishing sustainability disclosures in 2023. item.title: Tunisia looks to Seoul's 120 hotline as model for better public services
item.description: A public service hotline built to help Seoul residents navigate everything from transportation to welfare and taxes is attracting attention abroad, with governments looking to Korea’s capital for lessons in making administration more responsive. Seoul’s 120 Dasan Call Foundation said it had conducted 19 international exchanges between 2023 and October 2026, including 17 visits by foreign institutions and two cooperation agreements, sharing its experience with government agencies and public service organizations across several countries. Among its recent visitors were seven senior Tunisian government officials who toured the foundation on Nov. 12 as part of a training program under the Korea International Cooperation Agency’s project to upgrade Tunisia’s national civil petition system. During the visit, the foundation introduced its specialized consultation services, procedures for handling public grievances and efforts to improve citizen satisfaction, while explaining how data gathered through consultations can be analyzed and used to improve public policies. item.title: Suicide deaths fall 16.3 percent in September
item.description: The number of suicide deaths fell 16.3 percent from a year earlier to 1,014 in September, while the figure for the first nine months of the year dropped 11.7 percent on-year to 9,591, data from the Office for Government Policy Coordination showed Friday. Of September's total, men accounted for 69 percent, or 701 deaths, while women accounted for 31 percent, or 313 deaths. Across all regions, the total number of suicide deaths through September dropped from the same period last year, except for the central administrative city of Sejong, which saw a 27.3 percent increase in such deaths from a year ago, the data showed. The southern island of Jeju saw the biggest drop of 24.6 percent in suicide deaths this year, followed by the central city of Daejeon at 21.4 percent, and the southeastern cities of Ulsan and Daegu at 20.9 percent and 16.4 percent, respectively. Such sharp declines follow a series of anti-suicide measures by the Lee Jae Myung administration. Suicide prevention is part of Lee's broader goal of building what he has called an administration dedicated to saving lives. South Korea

item.title: KOGAS wins prime minister's award for helping small businesses go global
item.description: Korea Gas Corp. (KOGAS) has won a prime minister’s citation for turning its industrial expertise into a broader support network for smaller businesses, helping them develop domestic technology, enter overseas markets and reduce financing costs. The state-run energy company said Friday it received the award at the 2026 Shared Growth Week ceremony held at Coex Magok in Seoul on Thursday, recognizing its efforts to promote cooperation between large corporations and small and midsize enterprises. One of its major achievements was helping localize cryogenic ball bearings designed to operate at temperatures as low as minus 162 degrees Celsius, a technology previously dependent on imports. Under the initiative, a small business developed the technology while KOGAS opened its Pyeongtaek liquefied natural gas terminal as a testing site, providing opportunities for field trials and establishing a track record for commercial deliveries. The company also expanded its shared payment system, which guarantees more secure payments to smaller suppliers, recording 137.1 billion won ($95 million), up 190

item.title: Overseas card spending hits record high in Q3
item.description: South Koreans' overseas card spending hit the highest-ever amount in the third quarter of the year on the back of an increase in outbound travelers, data showed Friday. The amount of money spent overseas by South Koreans with credit and debit cards came to $6.63 billion in the July-September period, up 13.3 percent from three months earlier, according to data from the Bank of Korea (BOK). The on-quarter rise marks the sharpest since the first quarter of 2023, when the reading spiked 14.8 percent, and also is the largest-ever. The central bank said more South Koreans traveled overseas, although direct purchases from abroad declined. The number of overseas travelers came to 7.12 million in the third quarter of the year, up 7.4 percent from the previous quarter. The combined amount of purchases made through overseas shopping malls, on the other hand, fell 0.8 percent to $1.4 billion.

item.title: Pay-TV subscribers continue to decline; IPTV subscribers slightly up in H1: data
item.description: The number of pay-TV subscribers has declined for the past two years, while the number of people using Internet Protocol TV (IPTV) services has maintained a steady uptrend, data from the country's media watchdog showed Friday. The number of people subscribed to pay-TV services in South Korea fell 0.29 percent from the second half of 2025 to 36 million as of June this year, according to findings by the Korea Media and Communications Commission (KMCC). The number has been dropping since the second half of 2024, the KMCC said. In contrast, IPTV service subscribers inched up 0.47 percent from six months earlier to 21.6 million, accounting for over 60 percent of the market, according to the data. By company, KT accounted for the most with 25.39 percent, followed by SK Broadband with 18.67 percent and LG Uplus with 15.96 percent. The three companies are major fixed-line operators in South Korea. item.title: Market volatility expanding amid AI uncertainties: financial authorities
item.description: Global stocks are experiencing increasing volatility due to artificial intelligence (AI)-linked uncertainties, and there is a need to guard against the deepening ties between the chipmaking sector's cycle and the financial market, South Korean authorities said Friday. Earlier in the day, Finance Minister Lee Hyoung-il held a meeting with heads of the Bank of Korea, the Financial Services Commission (FSC) and other related agencies to check market conditions. The policymakers echoed views that the local stock market's volatility is growing due to uncertainties surrounding the AI sector and changes in the global trade environment. In particular, they said it needs to closely check the risks related to the correlation of the chip sector and the stock market. Last week, the financial authorities unveiled a set of steps to respond to stock market volatility, including lifting the limit of share buybacks by listed firms. item.title: Ex-President Yoon's senior aide gets suspended prison term over presidential residence relocation
item.description: A Seoul district court on Friday sentenced a former senior aide to former President Yoon Suk Yeol to a suspended prison term over irregularities in the 2022 relocation of the presidential residence. The Seoul Central District Court handed down a two-year prison sentence, suspended for three years, for former presidential chief of staff Kim Dae-ki after finding him guilty of abusing his power in connection with the case. It also sentenced former presidential secretary for administrative affairs Yoon Jae-soon and former presidential secretary for general affairs Kim Oh-jin to one-year prison terms, both suspended for two years. The officials were indicted on charges of illegally diverting 2.09 billion won ($1.56 million) from the interior ministry's budget to pay an interior design company for the renovation of the presidential residence following its relocation from Cheong Wa Dae to the central Seoul district of Yongsan. item.title: Lee Jong-suk proves he's still the romance king in 'The Remarried Empress'
item.description: Despite early criticism surrounding Disney+'s fantasy romance series "The Remarried Empress," Lee Jong-suk emerged as one of its biggest winners, winning over viewers with his romantic chemistry with Shin Min-a and reaffirming his reputation as a master of on-screen romance. The 10-episode series concluded with a happy ending as Empress Navier (Shin Min-a), after divorcing Emperor Sovieshu (Ju Ji-hoon), marries Heinrey (Lee Jong-suk) and embarks on a new chapter in her love life. Based on the popular web novel and webtoon of the same name, "The Remarried Empress" generated considerable anticipation ahead of its release for bringing romance fantasy, a genre widely popular in Korean digital comics and fiction but relatively uncommon in live-action K-dramas, to the screen. item.title: Korea expands customs tech footprint with Guatemala's launch of UNI-PASS system
item.description: Korea is extending its digital customs network into Central America, with Guatemala launching an electronic clearance system developed through a five-year cooperation project designed to speed up trade and strengthen customs enforcement. The Korea Customs Service said Friday that Guatemala officially opened its upgraded electronic customs system, known as UNI-PASS, at the headquarters of its tax authority, the Superintendency of Tax Administration, in Guatemala City on Thursday (local time). The ceremony was attended by Kim Ki-dong, director-general for information and data policy at the Korea Customs Service, Korean Ambassador to Guatemala Kim Deuk-hwan and Guatemalan tax chief Werner Ovalle, along with officials from both countries. The project, launched in 2022 as part of Korea’s official development assistance program, involved 6.9 billion won ($4.8 million) in support over five years. item.title: Sungkyunkwan University ranks 24th worldwide in THE Interdisciplinary Science Rankings
item.description: Sungkyunkwan University (SKKU) ranked 24th worldwide in the Times Higher Education (THE) Interdisciplinary Science Rankings 2027, highlighting its growing strength in interdisciplinary research. SKKU climbed 19 places from last year’s ranking of 43rd to become the top-ranked university in Korea. “This achievement reflects international recognition of our university members’ efforts to tackle societal challenges beyond disciplinary boundaries,” SKKU President Yoo Ji-beom said. “We will continue to advance as a global research-oriented university at the forefront of interdisciplinary research,” he added. A total of 1,058 universities worldwide were ranked in this year’s assessment, released by THE, a U.K.-based higher education ranking organization. Launched in 2024 by THE in partnership with Schmidt Science Fellows, the rankings assess universities’ contributions and commitment to interdisciplinary scientific research. item.title: HD Hyundai XiteSolution showcases parts at Asia's largest machinery expo
item.description: HD Hyundai XiteSolution, the intermediate holding company for HD Hyundai's construction equipment business, said Friday it showcased its core components at bauma China 2026 as it expands its global parts business. The exhibition ran from Tuesday through Friday in Shanghai. More than 4,000 companies from 30 countries took part, and organizers expect more than 300,000 visitors from 180 countries, making it Asia's largest construction machinery show. This is the first time the company's components business has exhibited on its own at an international trade fair. At a 180-square-meter booth at the Shanghai New International Expo Centre, the company displayed 22 products. The hydraulic components included eight hydraulic motors, four cylinders, three main control valves and one main pump, which are used in machines ranging from compact models to mid- and large-size equipment weighing dozens of tons. item.title: Cadillac launches Korean-designed Vistiq electric SUV in Korea
item.description: Cadillac has launched the Vistiq, an all-electric, three-row large SUV, in Korea. The model's design and engineering were led by GM's research and development arm in the country, the U.S. luxury automaker said Friday. GM Technical Center Korea led the development of the Vistiq, which went on sale first in North America. There, it picked up the nickname "Baby Escalade," after Cadillac's flagship full-size SUV. The Vistiq will be sold in Korea only in the top-end Platinum trim, priced at 181.7 million won after tax benefits for eco-friendly vehicles. The SUV is 5,235 millimeters long and 2,025 millimeters wide, with a 3,094-millimeter wheelbase. It seats six in three rows, with two seats in each row. A dual-motor all-wheel-drive system produces 615 horsepower and about 880 newton-meters of torque. The SUV goes from zero to 100 kilometers per hour in about 3.7 seconds, according to Cadillac's own testing. Its 102-kilowatt-hour battery provides a combined range of 430 kilometers per charge. It supports fast charging of up to 190 kilowatts. The SUV comes with the North American Charging Standa

item.title: N. Korean fishing boat repatriated, with 1 crewman opting to stay in S. Korea
item.description: South Korea sent a North Korean fishing boat back across the sea border Friday with six of its seven crew members aboard as one decided to stay, the unification ministry said. The vessel, found near Ulleung Island in the East Sea earlier this month, crossed the Northern Limit Line (NLL), the de facto maritime border, at 8:33 a.m. and met two North Korean ships waiting on the other side at 9 a.m., the ministry said. The boat was found adrift Nov. 3 in international waters north of the South Korean island. Of the seven North Korean men aboard, one expressed a wish to stay in the South. An official at the ministry said the man had made it clear from the outset that he did not want to go back to the North. The ministry decided to repatriate the six crewmen on humanitarian grounds. The remaining one will be protected in South Korea as a defector under relevant laws. Seoul contacted the North through the United Nations (U.N.) Command since the two sides have no working communication channel. The government also broadcast updates on its repatriation over the international maritime communications n

item.description: Chaevi, an electric vehicle (EV) fast-charging operator, signed a memorandum of understanding with commercial vehicle maker Tata Daewoo Mobility and parcel delivery firm Daeshin Parcel to expand the use of electric trucks in logistics, the company said Friday. The agreement was signed Thursday at Daeshin Parcel's Incheon office. Chaevi CEO Choi Young-hoon, Tata Daewoo Sales CEO Im Hyeong-jung and Daeshin Parcel President Park Byung-kwon attended. Daeshin Parcel will bring in the electric trucks and prepare its sites for charging. item.title: From metal type to AI: Korea's reading culture to be explored at MMCA
item.description: In an age of endless scrolling and artificial intelligence (AI)-generated text, why does reading still matter? The National Museum of Modern and Contemporary Art (MMCA), Korea, poses that question in "Ways of Reading," which opens on Friday at its Seoul branch. The exhibition retells the history of Korean graphic design and publishing since the 1970s through the everyday act of reading. The show will run through April 11 next year, featuring about 500 works and materials by roughly 40 teams. "Amid the flood of images that envelops us, this exhibition asks why reading remains valid," MMCA Director Ki Hye-kyung said during a press preview Thursday. She noted that the ongoing "text-hip" trend, in which young people share passages from books and images of themselves reading on social media, is itself "another facet of image culture built on reading." Curator Woo Hyun-jung said reading may seem immaterial, but it is a structure built from readers, letters, pages and the technology behind them. "What we read is not only text," she said. item.title: Korea's speed, Finland's lifelong learning could build human skills in AI age
item.description: As concerns mount over artificial intelligence (AI)-assisted cheating in examinations, educators and experts are calling for a fundamental rethink of how students are taught and assessed in the age of AI. The issue was a central topic at the Korea-Finland Innovation Forum 2026, held Wednesday at Korea University's SK Future Hall. Under the theme "Human Capabilities in the AI Age," academics, government officials and industry representatives explored how education must move beyond memorization to developing creativity and critical thinking. Welcoming participants, Finnish Ambassador to Korea Jyri Järviaho said AI would have a profound impact on future jobs and the skills required to perform them, making it essential for education systems to adapt to changing realities. "Our goal is to ensure that individuals and societies have the capabilities to thrive in the AI age by strengthening AI literacy, fostering trust in new technologies and encouraging the responsible adoption of AI," he said. item.title: Korea boosts commuter bus accessibility for people with disabilities
item.description: More than half of Korea’s city buses now feature low-floor designs, marking a significant step toward making public transportation more accessible to an aging population and people with mobility challenges. The Ministry of Land, Infrastructure and Transport said Friday that low-floor buses accounted for 51.8 percent of the nation’s city bus fleet in 2025, with 18,160 vehicles in operation. That represents an increase of 2,417 buses from the previous year, bringing the country past the 50 percent milestone. The progress comes as demand for accessible transportation continues to grow. According to the ministry’s 2025 transportation accessibility survey, 16.46 million people, or 32.2 percent of Korea’s population, were classified as having mobility challenges at the end of last year, up approximately 330,000 from 2024. The category covers a broad range of people, including those with disabilities, adults aged 65 and older, pregnant women, people accompanying children under 7 and children aged 12 or younger. Accessibility has improved across the country’s broader transportation infr

item.title: HUFS to build 1st inter-university dormitory among private universities
item.description: Hankuk University of Foreign Studies (HUFS) signed a memorandum of understanding with the Korea Advancing Schools Foundation on Monday to build an inter-university dormitory and improve its educational facilities. The agreement was signed by HUFS President Kang Kee-hoon and Lee Ha-woon, chairman of the foundation, at HUFS’ Seoul campus, the university said. The two institutions have agreed to build a privately funded Haengbok (Happy) Dormitory that will accommodate students from HUFS and nearby universities in Seoul, while improving the university’s educational environment and promoting sustainable development. The project is the first of its kind to be undertaken by a private university in Korea, HUFS said. Under the agreement, HUFS will provide the site behind the Humanities and Sciences Building on its Seoul campus free of charge to a special-purpose company (SPC) established by the foundation to build a dormitory that can accommodate about 400 students. The university will also work with the foundation to provide administrative and financial support for the project. The foundation

item.title: CSAT perfect scorers shun spotlight amid AI cheating suspicions
item.description: At least three students are believed to have earned perfect scores on this year's College Scholastic Ability Test (CSAT), yet they are shunning the spotlight for fear of being suspected of artificial intelligence (AI)-assisted cheating. The current tally of three is based on preliminary self-grading, with the number expected to rise when official results are released on Dec. 11. High schools and private academies have long been eager to publicize perfect scorers on Korea's high-stakes college entrance exam, with news of such achievements emerging as early as exam day last year. Their study habits, daily routines and university aspirations have often made headlines, while schools have celebrated their success as a source of pride. This year, however, even students who earned their scores legitimately are reluctant to come forward for fear of cheating allegations. The shift in sentiment follows an admission of AI-assisted cheating by the top scorer on the national tax accountant qualification exam, which has fueled widespread suspicion of high achievers across national exams. item.title: K-art takes center stage in Seoul with new wave of young talent
item.description: A new exhibition in central Seoul is betting that Korea’s next cultural export may come not from a music stage or television screen, but from the studios of its emerging contemporary artists. The Korea Tourism Organization (KTO) is opening “NEW WAVE,” a special exhibition showcasing works by 10 promising Korean artists, at HiKR Ground, its tourism promotion center in Jung District, Seoul, Friday. Running through March 30, 2027, the exhibition is being organized in partnership with the Galleries Association of Korea and will offer free admission at the center’s fourth-floor Local Ground gallery. item.title: Data reveals how medical tourists explore Korea beyond hospitals
item.description: Korea is looking to turn its booming medical tourism industry into a wider driver of regional tourism, using big data to understand where international patients travel, shop and spend beyond their hospital visits. The Korea Tourism Organization (KTO), in partnership with the Ministry of Culture, Sports and Tourism, hosted the third Korea Tourism Today Data Seminar at Coex in southern Seoul this week. Bringing together around 500 representatives from local governments, the tourism industry and academia, the event explored the current landscape and future growth potential of K-medical tourism through mobility and consumption data. The seminar presented an analysis of medical tourism spending across six major regions: Seoul, Busan, Daegu, Jeju, Gyeonggi Province and Incheon. Notably, medical tourism expenditure in Busan and Jeju surged 150.6 percent and 157.6 percent, respectively, in the first nine months of 2026 compared with the same period last year. On Wednesday, entrepreneur Choi Sun-jung, the daughter-in-law of veteran actress Sunwoo Eun-sook, shared footage on social media from an event celebrating the 24th anniversary of YÉOL, a foundation dedicated to preserving and promoting Korean cultural heritage. Song, who serves as an official ambassador for the foundation, attended the event as part of his efforts to raise awareness of Korea's cultural heritage. When the event's host, composer and television personality Joo Young-hoon, asked Song how he had been, the actor warmly replied, "Yes, it's been a long time." item.title: Exam misconduct cases rise 70% in this year's CSAT: ministry
item.description: The number of exam misconduct cases detected during this year's College Scholastic Ability Test (CSAT) rose nearly 70 percent from a year earlier, despite tighter exam management and oversight, the education ministry said Friday. Notably, cases involving smart devices rose 3.6-fold, accounting for nearly a quarter of all violations detected during the Nov. 19 exam, the ministry said. According to a report submitted to the National Assembly, a total of 474 cases of CSAT-related exam misconduct had been reported as of Wednesday, up 69.9 percent from 279 a year earlier. By category, the most common violations involved writing answers after the end-of-exam bell and breaches of answer-sheet rules during the fourth-period social studies session, with 127 cases each. The former surged from 25 cases last year, while the latter increased by 53. They were followed by violations involving smart devices, which jumped to 112 from 31, possession of electronic devices at 51 from 53 and other forms of misconduct, including failure to follow proctors' instructions at 57, up 38 from the previous year. item.title: N. Korean defector in custody after unauthorized entry into restricted front-line border area
item.description: A North Korean defector has been taken into police custody after entering a civilian restricted area near the inter-Korean border and is currently undergoing questioning, a military official said Friday. The military found the woman in her 30s at around 6:40 p.m. Thursday between a village north of the Civilian Control Line (CCL) and the general outpost fence in the border county of Cheorwon, about 75 kilometers northeast of Seoul, a Joint Chiefs of Staff (JCS) official said. Police and relevant authorities are questioning her over possible espionage linked to North Korea, among other suspicions, the JCS official said. The woman had crossed the CCL, which runs just south of the Demilitarized Zone (DMZ) separating the two Koreas, and was heading north toward the heavily fortified GOP area secured with barbed-wire fences, according to military officials. She had come as close as about 200 meters to the GOP line before being apprehended. item.title: Renault Filante targets drivers sensitive to ride comfort
item.description: For some drivers, ride comfort is decided by the smallest details — a bump over a speed hump, a manhole cover or a seam in the road. These minor impacts may go unnoticed at first, but once drivers become sensitive to them, they can become a constant part of the driving experience. Unlike horsepower or fuel economy, ride comfort is difficult to capture in a specification sheet. It depends on how a vehicle responds to different road surfaces and how effectively it keeps vibrations and noise away from occupants. Renault Korea’s flagship Filante crossover is designed around this everyday driving experience, with a focus on balancing comfort and stability across a wide range of road conditions. A key part of the setup is its frequency-sensitive damper, which is fitted as standard across the lineup. The system adjusts damping characteristics according to the frequency of vibrations generated by the road. On highways, for example, the system can reduce damping forces when dealing with small, rapid vibrations, helping filter out fine road imperfections. During winding-road driving or situati

item.title: Lee's approval rating rises for 2nd straight week: poll
item.description: President Lee Jae Myung's approval rating rose for the second consecutive week to 41 percent, a poll showed Friday. The survey, conducted by Gallup Korea from Tuesday through Thursday on 1,000 people aged 18 and older, showed that positive assessments of Lee's performance gained 1 percentage point from the previous week. Those who disapproved of Lee's handling of state affairs also rose 1 percentage point to 50 percent. Lee's approval rating has fluctuated between 39 and 41 percent for seven weeks since mid-October. Among those who positively assessed Lee's performance, 29 percent cited diplomacy, up from 24 percent the previous week, followed by economic and livelihood issues at 10 percent, and communication at 5 percent. Lee returned home last Thursday after attending the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) and the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summits, where he also held a series of bilateral talks. item.title: Korean mystery thriller 'White Blast' set for English-language remake
item.description: Korean mystery thriller "White Blast" is heading for a global audience, with an English-language remake officially confirmed and original director Hong Eui-jeong set to return behind the camera. The film, which continues to attract strong audience interest and critical praise in Korea, follows a mysterious death at a remote rural railway station cut off by heavy snowfall. As retirement approaches, veteran stationmaster Gap-soo (Kim Yoon-seok) finds himself caught up in an unsettling mystery alongside his newly appointed successor, Hyun-taek (Koo Kyo-hwan). The Canadian production company Rhombus Media will co-produce the remake with the original film’s production company, Lewis Pictures. Known for its collaborations with internationally acclaimed filmmakers, Rhombus Media has been behind projects including Park Chan-wook’s HBO series "The Sympathizer" and Denis Villeneuve’s "Enemy," starring Jake Gyllenhaal. item.title: Police raid justice ministry, prosecution over alleged records leak to lawmaker
item.description: Police on Friday raided the justice ministry and prosecution offices over allegations that investigative records were leaked to independent lawmaker Han Dong-hoon. The Seoul Metropolitan Police Agency sent investigators to search the ministry, the Supreme Prosecutors Office and the Seoul Western District Prosecutors Office and secure evidence related to the allegations. The ruling Democratic Party of Korea filed a complaint against Han in September on suspicion of disclosing official secrets after he raised lobbying allegations against then Justice Minister nominee Kim Seung-won. Han at the time unveiled a prosecution report about Kim's lobbying allegations, drawing questions over how he obtained the document. Kim later withdrew his candidacy amid growing controversy over the scandal.

Kim made the remarks the previous day during a photo session with participants of the Seventh Conference of Cell Secretaries of the Workers' Party of Korea (WPK), the Korean Central News Agency (KCNA) said. Cells are the party's most elementary units, with five to 30 members each. item.title: North Korean troops cross inter-Korean border about 40 times over past 2 months: lawmaker
item.description: North Korean troops have crossed the heavily fortified inter-Korean border on roughly 40 occasions over the past two months, a South Korean lawmaker said Friday, following September's mine blast in the Demilitarized Zone (DMZ) that injured three South Korean soldiers. The North violated the Military Demarcation Line (MDL) about 30 times in October and roughly 10 times this month, according to data submitted to Rep. Yu Yong-weon of the main opposition People Power Party. North Korean soldiers' border crossing has continued even after the Sept. 21 explosion of North Korea-planted mines south of the DMZ. Pyongyang has denied responsibility. Pyongyang has reinforced border fortification work by installing barbed-wire fences and land mines along the inter-Korean border. Such activities became evident after North Korean leader Kim Jong-un declared the relations between the two Koreas as those between "two hostile states". Under the rules of engagement, the South Korean military responds by airing warning broadcasts and firing warning shots in the event of MDL crossings. Earlier, the Joint Chief

item.title: Korea to co-chair vice finance ministers meeting of ASEAN+3 next year
item.description: Seoul's finance ministry said Friday that the country will co-chair the meeting of vice finance ministers and deputy central bankers of Korea, China, Japan and the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) next year. The Ministry of Economy and Finance said the ASEAN+3 Finance and Central Bank Deputies' Meeting will be held in Singapore in April and then in Seoul around November. Korea proposed to discuss financial stability amid the spread of artificial intelligence (AI) as next year's key agenda. Meanwhile, this year's meeting was held in Kyoto, Japan, on Wednesday and Thursday to discuss ways to strengthen regional financial cooperation. During the gathering, participants assessed that regional economic growth will be maintained on the back of AI-related investment despite regional tensions such as the Middle East war trends. They also discussed how to further develop the Chiang Mai Initiative Multilateralization (CMIM), a $240 billion currency-swap arrangement established in 2010 as a regional financial safety net. item.title: 2 Korean naval submarines under repair after accidents
item.description: Two of the Korean Navy's attack submarines are undergoing repairs after sustaining damage in separate accidents, military officials said Friday. One 1,800-ton Son Won Il-class submarine suffered damage to its protective hull coating after getting entangled in discarded fishing nets during a nighttime mission in the Yellow Sea in September, according to Navy officials. No casualties were reported. With its navigational systems intact, the vessel was able to return to its home port under its own power, the Navy said, adding that it is currently undergoing maintenance and repairs for restoration. Another submarine of the same class, the Hong Beom Do vessel, caught fire in April while undergoing a scheduled overhaul at a shipyard in the southeastern city of Ulsan, about 300 kilometers southeast of Seoul. The Navy has been assessing the damage and carrying out repairs on the vessel, noting that no timeline has been set for when the work will be completed. The incidents have raised concerns over a potential gap in naval operational readiness, as the Navy currently operates about 20 conventional

item.title: Why China is hesitating to send new pandas to Korea
item.description: Chinese Ambassador to Korea Dai Bing said Thursday that Beijing would find it difficult to approve Korea’s request for a pair of giant pandas for a zoo in Gwangju. He cited public backlash in China after the Gwangju Biennale allowed an exhibition to be called “Taiwan Pavilion.” Dai made the remarks during a press conference in central Seoul, following China's hosting of the 2026 Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in Shenzhen. "Pandas are China's national treasure and China has relevant laws and regulations on the protection of rare animals. Any loan must go through strict procedures in accordance with these regulations. More than 40 pandas are currently on loan to countries outside China," Dai said. He said Beijing initially had no strong view on where in Korea the pandas would go, but the biennale controversy drew a strong reaction in China. "The move ran directly counter to the Korean government's position of upholding the one-China principle and it triggered considerable opposition among the Chinese public. item.title: 'King is back': Nvidia boss's return sparks fresh AI deepfake deluge
item.description: WASHINGTON — Scandal-hit Jensen Huang's return as chief executive of U.S. chip giant Nvidia has triggered a fresh avalanche of AI-generated parody videos, highlighting how the sex-and-espionage saga has become a prime target for hyper-realistic deepfakes. Following his shock resignation amid revelations of extramarital affairs, including one with a woman suspected to be a Chinese spy, AI-created clips placing Huang in fabricated scenarios provoked amusement across social media -- and millions of views. The viral videos cast Huang in Bollywood-style gangster plots, song-and-dance routines and other scenes with the purported spy. Huang's reinstatement at the helm of the chipmaker, following an extraordinary intervention by President Donald Trump, triggered a fresh wave of parody clips across social media platforms, including Elon Musk's X. One clip depicted Huang replacing the late Iraqi dictator Saddam Hussein in an infamous video of a real-life purge. Smoking a cigar, Huang was portrayed calling out the names of alleged traitors in a crowded hall. "It's time to take revenge," read the c

item.title: Seoul stocks up over 2% Friday morning amid AI jitters
item.description: South Korean stocks traded sharply higher late Friday morning, extending a tentative recovery after a volatile week, led by gains in technology shares amid continued market jitters over artificial intelligence (AI). After opening 0.37 percent higher, the benchmark Korea Composite Stock Price Index (KOSPI) extended its earlier gains to trade up 105.42 points, or 2.24 percent, to 4,816.63 as of 11:20 a.m. Investors are watching whether the tech rally has staying power after days of volatility driven by doubts over the sustainability of the AI trade. Overnight, Wall Street was closed for the Thanksgiving holiday. In Seoul, large-cap shares were trading higher across the board. Market bellwether Samsung Electronics went up 1.98 percent and its chipmaking rival SK hynix gained 1.71 percent after both opened lower. Among other index heavyweights, SK Square, the parent of SK hynix, added 1.84 percent, while battery maker LG Energy Solution gained 3.15 percent. The Korean won was quoted at 1,341.3 won against the U.S. dollar as of 11:20 a.m., up 2.6 won from the previous stock trading session's clo

item.title: French cinema star Gérard Depardieu ordered to stand trial for rape and sexual assault
item.description: PARIS — Gérard Depardieu , for decades one of France’s most celebrated actors, has been ordered to stand trial on charges of raping and sexually assaulting a young actress, authorities said Thursday, less than two weeks after the cinema star abandoned his appeal of a sexual assault conviction in a separate case. Actress Charlotte Arnould was 22 when she accused Depardieu in 2018 of raping her at his Paris home. Eight years later, the Paris Court of Appeal ruled that the actor should face trial over allegations of rape and sexual assault on Aug. 7, 2018, while dismissing allegations relating to a second incident six days later. Depardieu, 77, has denied the rape allegations. His lawyer, Delphine Meillet, told The Associated Press that he disputes Thursday’s ruling, without specifying whether he would challenge it before France’s highest court for civil and criminal cases. The ruling upholds part of an investigating judge’s August 2025 decision to send Depardieu to trial. The case has become one of the most prominent in France’s reckoning with sexual violence , as the #MeToo mo

item.title: Musk pledges two SpaceX shares for every US child in $18 bil. AI charm offensive
item.description: Elon Musk plans to gift every child in the United States two SpaceX shares, as he attempts to build public support for his satellite and AI businesses during a period of intense public and political scrutiny of the technology sector. The world's richest person announced the share giveaway, which is worth a total of around $18 billion, on the eve of U.S. Thanksgiving and just hours after SpaceX won U.S. approval on Wednesday to deploy 1 million satellites for data centers in space. Musk is seeking to expand SpaceX's role in the AI industry, even as the rapid growth of computing infrastructure raises concern about its environmental impact and the economic and political influence of technology billionaires. Opponents of data center development were among the biggest winners for the Democrats in this month's U.S. midterm elections. "The initiative clearly helps broaden public participation in the SpaceX story," Chez Anbu, head of wealth advisory at OCBC in Singapore, said on Thursday. "Giving children a direct economic stake in the company creates a powerful narrative around broader participa

item.title: N. Korea's Kim attends Russian troupe's Pyongyang show amid deepening ties
item.description: North Korean leader Kim Jong-un has watched a Russian art troupe performance in Pyongyang, state media reported Friday, the latest sign of deepening ties between the two countries. Kim attended the show the previous day at the East Pyongyang Grand Theater with a Russian government delegation currently visiting North Korea for the 13th meeting of the two countries' intergovernmental committee on trade, economic, scientific and technological cooperation, the Korean Central News Agency (KCNA) said. Kim's wife, Ri Sol-ju, was seen with him, as were Jo Yong-won, a party secretary, and Yun Jong Ho, minister of external economic relations. Russian singer Larisa Dolina and musicians from the Osipov State Academic Russian Folk Orchestra performed. Speakers at the event called the show an opportunity to deepen "the traditional friendly relations" between the two peoples and to broaden "exchange and cooperation in various fields." item.title: Thanksgiving storm knocks out power, disrupts flights on US East Coast
item.description: A powerful storm disrupted the Thanksgiving holiday along much of the U.S. East Coast on Thursday, knocking out power for hundreds of thousands of users as wind gusts of up to 70 mph (112 kph) toppled trees and power lines. Storms contributed to flight delays, with FlightAware reporting a total of 417 U.S.-related cancellations on Thursday and some 1,800 delayed by Thursday afternoon. Major airports in the Washington and New York City areas were among the hardest hit. Heavy rains flooded coastal areas, while utilities warned that rain-soaked ground and strong winds could increase the risk of falling trees and power outages. More than 836,000 U.S. utility customers had no power as of 4:06 p.m. ET (2106 GMT), including more than 174,000 in Virginia, 172,000 in Maryland and almost 170,000 in Pennsylvania, according to poweroutage.us. Its data also showed more than 117,000 outages in Missouri, over 91,000 in New Jersey, more than 20,000 in Delaware and nearly 16,000 in North Carolina. Utilities and state officials had warned the combination of strong onshore winds and rain could cause widesp

item.title: Trump uses Thanksgiving message to lash out at political foes, immigrants, federal government
item.description: As American families gathered to celebrate one of the biggest holidays of the year, U.S. President Donald Trump on Thursday used the occasion of Thanksgiving to attack liberals, immigrants and a federal agency. In a message on his Truth Social platform, Trump offered holiday greetings to people he accused of fraud, error or criminality. "I would like to wish a very Happy Thanksgiving to all of those people that have worked so hard to bring our Country to the Radical Far Left," Trump said in the 461-word post. The message was issued while the Republican president spent the family-oriented holiday at his Trump International Golf Club in West Palm Beach, Florida. He was expected to call U.S. service members later on Thursday from his Mar-a-Lago estate. In the holiday greeting, Trump accused his own government of falsifying U.S. economic data. item.title: Banks' earnings edge up through Sept. on rise in interest income
item.description: South Korean banks' net profit increased slightly in the first nine months of the year from a year earlier on the back of a rise in interest income, data showed Friday. The combined net profit of 20 banks came to 21.5 trillion won ($16 billion) in the January-September period, up 500 billion won, or 2.1 percent, from 21 trillion won in net profit recorded a year earlier, according to the data from the Financial Supervisory Service (FSS). Their interest income came to 48.4 trillion won in the first three quarters, up 3.7 trillion won, or 8.2 percent, from a year earlier. Non-interest income came to 5.9 trillion won in the January-September period, down 900 billion won, or 12.9 percent, over the cited period, according to the FSS. Their costs to cover loan losses came in at 4.9 trillion won in the January-September period, up 100 billion won, or 3.1 percent, from a year before. item.title: Insurance firms' lending down in Q3: data
item.description: Loans extended by insurance companies here fell in the third quarter of this year from three months earlier due to a fall in lending to both households and companies, data showed Friday. Insurers' outstanding loans reached 263.9 trillion won ($196.6 billion) as of end-September, down 2.1 trillion won from three months earlier, according to the data from the Financial Supervisory Service. The on-quarter fall was attributed to a decline in loans extended to households as well as to companies. Their household lending stood at 135.8 trillion won as of end-September, down 0.3 trillion won from the previous quarter, and corporate lending also fell 1.8 trillion won to 128 trillion won over the cited period. The loan delinquency rate, which measures the proportion of loan principal or interest unpaid for at least a month, stood at 1.27 percent at end-June, up 0.19 percentage point from three months earlier, according to the financial watchdog. The rate of insurers' nonperforming loans came to 1.42 percent at the end of September, up 0.11 percentage point from three months earlier, the latest find

item.title: AI bruise-measuring tool wins top prize at public safety contest
item.description: A sticker that helps police use artificial intelligence (AI) to document injuries in suspected abuse cases won the top prize at a national invention contest for public servants, the Ministry of Intellectual Property said Thursday. Other winning designs included a chair that screens for drugs concealed on the body without a hands-on search and floating beacons that guide people off tidal flats as the tide comes in. The ministry announced the winners of the 2026 Public Safety Invention Challenge at an awards ceremony at the National Assembly. It co-hosted the ceremony with the Korea Customs Service, the Korean National Police Agency, the National Fire Agency, the Korea Forest Service, the Korea Coast Guard and Reps. Jang Chul-min and Jeon Eun-su. Now in its ninth year, the contest invites employees from the five agencies to develop inventions that address safety problems they encounter on the job. item.title: KAI needs private ownership to compete in global market, defense consultant says
item.description: A veteran of the European defense industry says the Korea Aerospace Industries (KAI) should move into private hands so it can invest for the long term and warns that the KF-21 fighter jet may struggle to find buyers abroad without that stability. Alfred Kong, president of Suez Communication, said in an interview with The Korea Times that developing the KF-21 has earned Korea recognition among aerospace companies, but that the aircraft’s export prospects remain uncertain. “I don’t think the fighter will be a big seller, but it could help raise South Korea’s profile,” Kong said. Kong worked on bids to sell the Rafale and Eurofighter to Korea and was involved in the country’s acquisition of Taurus missiles and Airbus aerial refueling aircraft. He said steady production by Korean suppliers helped manufacturers deliver tanks and howitzers to Poland quickly. KAI privatization Established aircraft manufacturers can offer buyers local production and broader industrial partnerships as part of a deal, Kong said.
