item.title: Seoul Arts Center emerges as premier global arts tourism destination
item.description: In southern Seoul’s Seocho District, a unique cultural corridor awaits travelers — one where grand Western symphonies meet the deep, resonant rhythms of traditional Korean music. Anchored by the Seoul Arts Center (SAC), the beating heart of Korea’s performing arts, and the neighboring National Gugak Center, the home of traditional Korean music, this district is rapidly positioning itself as a must-visit hub for international cultural tourists. On Thursday, the Seoul Tourism Organization (STO) held a backstage tour to showcase the area's potential as a high-end tourism product. Joined by inbound travel agencies from the Seoul Arts Tourism Alliance, foreign influencers from the Global Seoul Mates and members of the media, the tour explored how SAC and its surrounding landmarks can be woven into an immersive, stay-type arts itinerary. item.title: Bourse operator activates sell-side sidecar for KOSPI on sharp fall
item.description: South Korea's bourse operator on Monday activated a sell-side sidecar for the benchmark Korea Composite Stock Price Index (KOSPI) as the market came under heavy selling pressure. Program trading for the KOSPI-listed shares was suspended for five minutes from 11:33 a.m., according to the Korea Exchange (KRX). The measure was triggered for a second consecutive session. The KOSPI shed 248.96 points, or 5.11 percent to 4,211.00 as of 11:34 a.m. The KOSPI came under heavy downward pressure as investors tracked Wall Street losses amid concerns over the artificial intelligence (AI) sector. A sell-side sidecar is triggered when the KOSPI 200 Futures Index falls 5 percent or more for at least one minute.

item.title: GS25 expands into Cambodia with goal of 500 convenience stores
item.description: GS25 is taking its Korean convenience store formula to Cambodia, opening its first store in Phnom Penh and setting an ambitious target of more than 500 outlets in the country within 10 years. GS Retail, operator of the convenience store chain, said Monday it had signed a master franchise agreement with Cambodian company META Retail, expanding its overseas operations to three countries following Vietnam and Mongolia. The agreement followed more than a year of local market research and feasibility studies by the two companies. The first store, GS25 Olympic Stadium, opened Friday in the Cambodian capital, offering about 3,000 products, including the chain’s private-label brands Yours and Real Price. Korean products account for about 50 percent of its food selection, with offerings ranging from fish-shaped pastries known as "bungeoppang" and Korean snacks to ready-to-eat meals and triangular "gimbap." item.title: Judges' representative warns against DPK's push to impeach chief justice
item.description: A representative of judges nationwide has strongly criticized the ruling Democratic Party of Korea's push to impeach the Supreme Court chief justice, calling on his fellow judges to stand up against any attempt to undermine judicial independence. Kang Dong-won, a senior judge at the Seoul Family Court who also chairs the National Conference of Judge Representatives, issued the rebuke in a message posted on the court's internal network, CourtNet, on Sunday, accusing the DPK of "going beyond the bounds." The DPK announced its decision to seek the impeachment of Supreme Court Chief Justice Cho Hee-dae after the top court on Thursday partially overturned an appellate ruling that sentenced former Prime Minister Han Duck-soo to 15 years in prison for playing a key role in former President Yoon Suk Yeol's failed martial law bid. The ruling party has since dropped Thursday's ruling from its list of impeachment grounds, instead citing the top court's alleged compliance with Yoon's martial law declaration, its decision to send President Lee Jae Myung's election law case back to the appeals court

item.title: Nat'l Assembly speaker to visit Japan, Australia to discuss parliamentary ties
item.description: National Assembly Speaker Cho Jeong-sik was set to embark on a seven-day trip to Japan and Australia on Monday to discuss ways to increase parliamentary cooperation, his office said. In Japan, Cho is scheduled to meet with Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi to discuss ways to expand parliamentary cooperation following the resumption of "shuttle diplomacy" between the countries' leaders, according to the office. He will also meet with Eisuke Mori, speaker of the House of Representatives, and House of Councilors President Masakazu Sekiguchi. During the meetings, Cho plans to propose resuming the "Future Dialogue between the Parliaments of Korea and Japan," a parliamentary dialogue forum last held in 2018, as part of efforts to restore regular communication channels between the two parliaments. item.title: Presidential office weighs extending restraining order against stalkers
item.description: The presidential office said Monday it is considering extending the period of restraining orders against stalkers as part of an initiative aimed at strengthening public safety and cracking down on crimes targeting vulnerable people. The initiative was announced by Cheong Wa Dae last week in response to growing public alarm over a series of relationship-based crimes and crimes with apparently random motives. The presidential office had said at the time that one of the measures under consideration was introducing life imprisonment without parole. "We will respond more strongly to crimes targeting the socially weak, including relationship-based crimes," presidential spokesperson Kim Sung-wan said at a press briefing, noting Wednesday will mark the start of the Week for the Elimination of Violence against Women, an annual government-designated campaign. item.title: New police chief vows to earn public trust in investigations
item.description: The new head of the National Police Agency (NPA) vowed Monday to make efforts to earn public trust in investigations as police take on a bigger role after the recent reform to the criminal justice system. NPA Commissioner General Kim Jong-chul made the pledge at his inauguration after Korea last month stripped prosecutors of their investigative powers, expanding the police role in criminal investigations. "Police will regard the criminal justice system reform as not an increase of authority but an expansion of grave responsibility," he said. "(I) will ensure the new criminal justice system is swiftly established and work to make police investigations more trusted." Kim, a former deputy NPA chief, fills the post that had been vacant for nearly two years since his predecessor was suspended from duty over his role in former President Yoon Suk Yeol's failed 2024 martial law bid. President Lee Jae Myung approved Kim's appointment Friday.

item.title: Busan rallies global scientists in bid to host 2033 biochemistry congress
item.description: Busan is rallying leading life sciences researchers behind a bid to host a major international scientific congress in 2033, aiming to bring 5,000 specialists from about 80 countries to the southern port city. The Busan Metropolitan Government, Busan Tourism Organization, Inje University and the exhibition center BEXCO are teaming up with the Korean Society for Biochemistry and Molecular Biology (KSBMB) to secure the hosting of the International Union of Biochemistry and Molecular Biology (IUBMB) Congress. As part of the effort, KSBMB and Inje University will hold an international academic advisory appointment ceremony and commemorative symposium Tuesday at Ananti at Busan Cove in Gijang. Four prominent scientists will be appointed as international academic advisers, including Kaang Bong-kiun, Koh Gou-young, Narry Kim and Chun Jang-soo, will participate as international academic advisers. Their research has appeared in leading scientific journals, including Cell, Nature and Science. item.title: 'White Blast' tops box office in first weekend
item.description: The Korean film "White Blast" debuted at No. 1 at the local box office, attracting more than 300,000 moviegoers in its first weekend. The film garnered 310,000 admissions from Friday to Sunday, accounting for 39.6 percent of ticket sales at theaters nationwide, according to the Korean Film Council on Monday. Released Nov. 18, "White Blast" is a black comedy thriller set at a remote train station isolated by heavy snow. It follows retiring station master Gap-soo (Kim Yoon-seok) and his successor Hyun-taek (Koo Kyo-hwan) as they discover a body inside a railway tunnel while on patrol and grow suspicious of each other. It was co-directed by Hong Eui-jeong, known for "Voice of Silence" (2020), and newbie director Park Sun-woo. The Japanese animated film "Chiikawa the Movie: The Secret of the Mermaid Island," which had held the No. 1 spot for six consecutive weeks through the previous weekend, fell to second place with around 91,000 admissions. The film garnered 310,000 admissions from Friday to Sunday, accounting for 39.6 percent of ticket sales at theaters nationwide, according to the Korean Film Council on Monday. Released Nov. 18, "White Blast" is a black comedy thriller set at a remote train station isolated by heavy snow. It follows retiring station master Gap-soo (Kim Yoon-seok) and his successor Hyun-taek (Koo Kyo-hwan) as they discover a body inside a railway tunnel while on patrol and grow suspicious of each other. It was co-directed by Hong Eui-jeong, known for "Voice of Silence" (2020), and newbie director Park Sun-woo. item.title: YouTube, Sunfull urge Korean youth to pause before posting online
item.description: Students across Korea are being urged to pause before hitting "post" as a nationwide anti-cyberbullying campaign expands to tackle artificial intelligence (AI)-generated content, organizers said Monday. The Sunfull Foundation and YouTube launched the Just a Moment campaign during a joint declaration ceremony at the National Assembly in Seoul on Friday, where they also recognized top contributors and outlined their 2026 initiatives. The event was co-hosted by the foundation and Rep. Kang Kyung-sook, with support from YouTube. Now in its third year, the campaign encourages internet users to pause for a few seconds and reconsider before sharing posts or leaving comments. This year, organizers expanded its digital literacy education beyond combating malicious comments to include helping young people distinguish AI-generated content. Students in classrooms nationwide watched campaign videos featuring actress Hye-ri and EBS character Pengsoo, joining in the message: “Pause for just a moment before you press the button!” The foundation also partnered with YouTube on in-person digital literacy

item.title: Sejong University study sheds light on role of cell death in plant immunity
item.description: A Sejong University research team has published a collaborative international study shedding new light on how plants use a form of cell death to fight infections and how the rice blast fungus uses a similar process to infect plants. The study, published in the international journal iMeta, was led by Jwa Nam-soo, a professor in the university’s Department of Integrative Bioscience and Biotechnology. Researcher Nam Khoa Nguyen was listed as a co-first author, while Jwa was a co-corresponding author. The paper, titled “Decoding ferroptosis via integrated multi-omics analyses in rice blast,” examines ferroptosis, a form of regulated cell death caused by iron-dependent oxidation of lipids, or fats, in cell membranes. Using integrated multi-omics analyses, the researchers identified contrasting roles of ferroptosis in plant immune responses and in the rice blast fungus’s infection process. They also proposed a model linking iron metabolism, reactive oxygen species, lipid oxidation and calcium signaling. The study builds on Jwa’s long-standing research into plant immune-related cell de

item.title: Personal information of more than 8,000 clients at Samsung Securities breached
item.description: Personal data belonging to over 8,000 clients of Samsung Securities has been breached, the brokerage said Monday, in the latest cyberattack against Korean financial firms. Samsung Securities said unauthorized access was detected on its customer response website last Saturday and the data breach did not affect other customer information beyond the affected system. Customer names, physical addresses and other personal information were compromised, Samsung Securities said. The brokerage said it reported the incident to the relevant authorities, who have been scrambling to deal with data breaches in recent months. The firm then said it has moved to strengthen its cybersecurity systems.

item.title: LS Cable secures record $500 mil. US export deal
item.description: LS Cable & System has secured a 700 billion won ($500 million) order to supply and install high-voltage cables for a major power grid project in New York, marking the largest U.S. export project ever won by a Korean cablemaker. The company said Monday that its U.S. subsidiary, LS Cable Systems America, will supply and install 345-kilovolt (kV) extra-high-voltage underground and submarine cable systems for the Propel NY Energy project. The project, jointly developed by the New York Power Authority (NYPA) and transmission developer New York Transco, involves building an approximately 145-kilometer (90-mile) transmission network linking Long Island with Queens and the Bronx in New York City, as well as Westchester County. It aims to expand transmission capacity, improve grid reliability and facilitate the integration of renewable energy sources, including offshore wind power. The project moved closer to construction after the New York State Public Service Commission approved construction plans for its first and second phases on Thursday. item.title: Korea asks Qatar to prioritize LNG supplies once production, shipping normalize
item.description: Industry Minister Kim Jung-kwan on Monday requested that Qatar give priority to supplying liquefied natural gas (LNG) to Korea when Qatari LNG production and navigation through the Strait of Hormuz return to normal, the ministry said. During a meeting with Qatari Minister of State for Energy Affairs Saad Sherida al-Kaabi in Seoul, Kim stressed that the Middle Eastern country is a key partner for Korea in the LNG sector and that cooperation between the two countries is crucial to ensuring a stable energy supply, according to the Ministry of Trade, Industry and Resources. He asked Qatar to prioritize Korea in LNG supplies once conditions return to normal. item.title: Zerobaseone to release new album in January
item.description: K-pop boy group Zerobaseone will return with a new album on Jan. 18, 2027. The group revealed the release date at the end of its performance at the 2026 MAMA Awards in Osaka, Japan, on Saturday, displaying a sign reading "Jan. 18, 2027." The upcoming release will be Zerobaseone's first full-group album in eight months, following its sixth EP, "Ascend-," released in May. The album's title and tracklist have not yet been disclosed. Zerobaseone, now a five-member group, has balanced group activities with unit and solo projects both at home and in Japan this year.

item.description: A father and daughter detained by masked immigration officers on an airport jet bridge in Seattle , causing chaos in front of other passengers, were heading to a family baptism ceremony in California, their lawyer said Sunday. Other passengers boarding the Alaska Airlines flight at Seattle-Tacoma International Airport on Saturday used their cellphones to film the father and daughter being detained by the officers, who were wearing unmarked jackets and khaki pants. The recordings were widely viewed on social media. The videos show the officers struggling with someone on the ground. The flight, bound for Los Angeles, was delayed. item.title: Exports more than double in 1st 20 days of November, with chip shipments surging to new high
item.description: Korea's exports more than doubled during the first 20 days of November, with shipments of semiconductors surging to a record high, customs data showed Monday. Outbound shipments reached $77.4 billion in the Nov. 1-20 period, up from $38.4 billion a year ago, according to the data from the Korea Customs Service. It marked the highest figure for the first 20 days of any month. The daily average export value in terms of business days also reached $4.84 billion, the highest for the first 20 days of any month. The combined exports from Jan. 1 through Friday came to $1.01 trillion, up 63.2 percent from a year earlier. Imports also jumped 39.4 percent on-year to $50.3 billion over the cited period, resulting in a trade surplus of $27.1 billion. By sector, exports of chips nearly quadrupled to $38.5 billion, setting a fresh record for the 20-day period. As a result, chip exports accounted for 49.7 percent of the country's total outbound shipment, a sharp increase of 24.3 percentage points from a year earlier. item.title: Seoul shares extend losses late Monday morning on AI-driven tech sell-off
item.description: South Korean shares extended their losses late Monday morning as a global technology rout intensified, with foreign investors turning net sellers and offloading major chip shares. After opening 2.77 percent lower, the benchmark Korea Composite Stock Price Index (KOSPI) fell 210.63 points, or 4.33 percent, to 4,659.33 as of 11:20 a.m. Foreign investors, who had been net buyers early in the session, shifted to net selling, further adding to downward pressure on the index. On Friday (local time), U.S. stocks tumbled amid intensified concerns over heavy investments by big tech firms in artificial intelligence (AI) infrastructure. In Seoul, chip stocks led the decline. Market bellwether Samsung Electronics fell 4.72 percent, while its chipmaking rival SK hynix declined 4.13 percent. Among other index heavyweights, battery maker LG Energy Solution slid 3.26 percent, and pharmaceutical giant Samsung Biologics fell 5.61 percent. The Korean won was quoted at 1,346.5 won against the U.S. dollar as of 11:20 a.m., up 0.5 won from the previous session's close.

item.title: Lee's approval rating rises for 2nd straight week to 37.3%: poll
item.description: President Lee Jae Myung's approval rating rose for the second consecutive week last week to 37.3 percent, a poll showed Monday. In a poll conducted on 2,514 adults nationwide from last Monday to Friday by Realmeter, positive assessments of Lee's job performance rose by 0.9 percentage point from the previous week, while negative assessments fell 1 percentage point to 59.9 percent. Realmeter attributed the rise in Lee's approval rating to diplomatic and economic achievements, including his attendance at the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) and the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summits in the Philippines and China, respectively, as well as his meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping on the sidelines of the APEC summit. The pollster also cited South Korea's exports topping the US$1 trillion mark as a positive factor but said domestic concerns, such as the KOSPI stock market index falling below 5,000 points and the recent controversy over artificial intelligence (AI)-assisted cheating on the college entrance exam, held back further gains in his approval rating. item.title: N. Korea's Kim says Pyongyang seeks no regional dominance, defending arms buildup as self-defense
item.description: North Korea does not seek regional dominance or expansion, leader Kim Jong-un has said, defending its military buildup as the exercise of its sovereign right, state media reported Monday. Kim made the remarks at a ceremony Sunday, where he received credentials from newly appointed ambassadors from Russia, Sweden, Indonesia, Vietnam, Brazil, the Czech Republic, India, the Philippines, Thailand and Bangladesh, according to the Korean Central News Agency (KCNA). He described a world growing more unstable and unpredictable, one in which some countries put their own interests above international law and trample the sovereignty of others. "The security situation in the DPRK and the political and military environment in East Asia urgently demand that we provide for ourselves the power and capability with which we can be fully ensured of security and confidence in peace," he said, defending Pyongyang's drive to expand its arsenal. item.title: Ateez scores 4th No. 1 on Billboard 200 with 'Golden Hour: Part. 6'
item.description: K-pop boy group Ateez has claimed its fourth No. 1 on the U.S. Billboard's main albums chart with its new album, "Golden Hour: Part. 6." Billboard reported in a chart preview Sunday (local time) that "Golden Hour: Part. 6" secured the top spot this week over albums from big-name stars, such as Olivia Rodrigo and Morgan Wallen. It marks the group's fourth No. 1 on the chart, following "The World Ep. Final: Will" in 2023, "Golden Hour: Part. 2" in 2024 and "Golden Hour: Part. 5" in July of this year. Including the latest release, Ateez has logged 10 consecutive albums on the Billboard 200. With 10 top-10 entries in the 2020s, it now has the most top 10s among groups this decade. Team leader Hongjoong said through the group's agency, KQ Entertainment, that he was "overwhelmed and grateful" to have earned the group's fourth No. 1 on the Billboard 200, crediting Atiny, the group's fandom, for the feat. item.title: US seeks answers on Nvidia's sale of chips to China, Bessent says
item.description: WASHINGTON — The US is seeking answers from Nvidia on its chip sales to China and will find out who was in charge of compliance at the company formerly led by Jensen Huang, who resigned following an affair with a suspected Chinese spy, US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said on Sunday. "We've been in touch with the temporary management, with the lead directors, with their lawyers, and we do need answers.... It behooves Nvidia to move quickly on this because we want to know what the culture was," Bessent told the CBS program "Face the Nation." Reports about Huang's relationship with a woman whom US intelligence suspects of being a Chinese spy and his extramarital affair with a company executive led to his resignation and investigations by US regulators and the FBI, congressional action, an internal review and a proposed investor class-action lawsuit. item.title: Russia starts towing ship hit by drones in Baltic, Finland says
item.description: HELSINKI — A Russian rescue vessel on Sunday began towing a Russian-owned cargo ship that was struck by drones in the Baltic Sea out of Finnish waters after two days of firefighting, Finland's coast guard said. The Finnish military has said the strike on the Sparta II on Saturday was likely carried out by Ukraine and that the vessel later drifted into Finnish waters. The 16 crew members were evacuated onto a nearby Russian ship. One crew member was slightly injured. "Thermal cameras show that some containers are warm, but the vessel is stable enough for towing to begin," Finland's coast guard said in a statement. It said that responsibility for the rescue will transfer to Russia once the ship leaves Finnish waters. Pictures and video released earlier by the Finnish coast guard showed several vessels spraying the Sparta II with water cannons during the night in a bid to put out the flames and cool down containers stacked on its deck. "Thermal cameras show that some containers are warm, but the vessel is stable enough for towing to begin," Finland's coast guard said in a statement. It said that responsibility for the rescue will transfer to Russia once the ship leaves Finnish waters. Pictures and video released earlier by the Finnish coast guard showed several vessels spraying the Sparta II with water cannons during the night in a bid to put out the flames and cool down containers stacked on its deck. item.title: Can climate diplomacy build on collapse of COP31?
item.description: ANTALYA, Turkey — The collapse of COP31 talks in Turkey on Sunday without a political agreement left exhausted negotiators questioning the future of a process that for three decades has led the global fight against climate change. For the small, vulnerable countries most exposed to rising sea levels and the increasingly extreme weather scientists link to rising carbon emissions, annual UN conferences are their chance to draw the world's attention to their plight and seek financial help. But the failure of the Turkish talks, which follows on from weak outcomes at other COPs in recent years, lays bare the need for change. Andres Martin Garrido Sanchez, director of environment in Peru's Ministry of Foreign Affairs, said "the credibility of the process" was at stake. "This system needs in-depth reforms," he said. Simon Stiell, the UN climate chief representing the UN convention that underpins international climate talks, said the consensus-based system can still function, but work was needed. "I have taken steps in engaging external knowledge leaders in advising on areas of potential reform.

item.title: Like SpaceX, Anthropic ran an unusual IPO process, chafing some bankers
item.description: NEW YORK — For the second time this year, Wall Street bankers and lawyers took home a massive paycheck from a record-setting initial public offering. And for the second time this year, some of them came out of it complaining in private about how the process was riddled with complications and unlike any they had worked on before. With SpaceX’s IPO in June, in which banks earned half a billion dollars in fees, bankers chafed over how tightly the Elon Musk-led company controlled the months-long process and kept financial and other information private, making it hard for advisers to do their jobs. item.title: 'The Remarried Empress' shows IP synergy as Disney+ hit lifts webtoon views
item.description: Global views for the webtoon "The Remarried Empress" surged 35-fold following the premiere of its Disney+ drama adaptation, highlighting the growing synergy between Korean web content and global streaming platforms. During the two weeks from Nov. 3 to 16, global views for the original webtoon jumped about 35 times compared to the two-week period from Aug. 12 to 25, right before the drama's teaser trailer was released, Naver Webtoon, a digital comics platform operated by Webtoon Entertainment, said Sunday. Viewership increased across all available languages, with Korean-language views soaring 54-fold and English-language views climbing 35-fold. Naver added that downloads and views for the original web novel on Naver Series jumped roughly 45-fold during the same period. Set in a fictional Western country, the romance fantasy follows Navier (Shin Min-a), the empress of the Eastern Empire, who agrees to a divorce demanded by Emperor Sovieshu (Ju Ji-hoon) on the condition that she can remarry Heinrey (Lee Jong-suk), a prince from the neighboring Western Kingdom. item.title: ALL'N wants violin to be hook, not gimmick, in K-pop
item.description: Strings are no strangers to K-pop, usually brought in to lend drama to a track's intro or swell beneath its bridge. Singer-violinist ALL'N, however, asks the instrument to do something harder and more important — carry most of a song's hook. On "Four Seasons," the title track of his first mini album of the same name, out Monday, the violin opens the song, answers the chorus and takes over the final post-chorus, doing the work a vocal hook usually would. "It's easy to add a violin section that sounds impressive, but I want a hook that someone remembers and wants to hear again," the 32-year-old told The Korea Times in a written interview. For the classically trained violinist, who also writes, produces and runs his own agency, the album caps a debut year spent testing how far the instrument can go inside a pop song. "I didn't want the violin to be something I brought out briefly to surprise people," he said. "I wanted it to be part of how they recognized my music." item.title: We Need a Third Reconstruction: Bishop William Barber Pushes Democrats to Take Action After Midterms
item.description:
With Democrats preparing to take control of both houses of Congress in January, Bishop William Barber of Repairers of the Breach argues the coalition that delivered the Democrats their midterm victories must now hold the incoming Congress accountable and keep organizing from the ground up. He and other faith leaders are calling on members of the incoming Congress to join them outside the U.S. Capitol next month to sign “A Pledge for Moral Defiance” — a commitment to pass legislation that addresses the needs of poor and working people and other vulnerable communities. Barber is pushing for what he describes as a Third Reconstruction: a sweeping moral and political agenda that includes a living wage, universal healthcare, protecting voting rights, affordable housing, environmental justice and comprehensive immigration reform.

“This was a vote not for Democrats,” says Barber. “It was a vote to say, 'Will you use policy to answer the pain that we are experiencing in this country at this particular moment?'”

item.title: "A Shameful Failure": U.N. Climate Summit Collapses as Final Text Drops Mention of Fossil Fuels
item.description:
The United Nations climate summit in Turkey, known as COP31, collapsed on Sunday after nations failed to reach an agreement on a new climate deal. A number of countries opposed the final draft because it made no mention of fossil fuels. Many poorer countries also objected to the lack of financial commitments from richer nations to assist them in adapting to the climate crisis.

“This is not about the Global South begging for assistance and help,” says Filipino climate activist Lidy Nacpil. “The principle is that [wealthy nations] have created this problem, and they have to contribute to the solutions.”

“What we’ve seen over the past decades is the Global North are not delivering on any of their responsibilities,” says Brandon Wu, director of policy and campaigns at ActionAid USA. “That’s what’s causing the deadlock. It’s not new to this COP, but it’s becoming increasingly untenable.”

We also speak with two other leading climate justice advocates who attended COP31, Tasneem Essop of Climate Action Network International and Kathy Jetn̄il-Kijiner, climate envoy of the Marshall Islands.

item.title: Bethlehem: Every saved child is a small miracle
item.description:
Babies abandoned in plastic bags, children found near dumpsters, or newborns whose mothers had to give them up to save their own lives... This is the reality that Slovak Sister Františka Lukačková DC, encounters every day in Bethlehem. For more than seven years, she has been serving at the Holy Family Crèche, the only institution of its kind in Palestine for found and abandoned children up to six years of age.

Donors from as far away as Spain and Poland have also contributed generously to providing food for the most needy.

item.title: "Little Hands, Big Change": 8-Year-Old Kenyan Climate Champion Marren Akeyo Speaks Out at COP31
item.description: At the U.N. climate summit in Antalya, Turkey, Little Miss Environment Kenya 2026, Marren Akeyo, addressed world leaders on their responsibility to take real action to stop climate change. “Climate change does not ask for your birth certificate before affecting you. So, why should we wait until we’re adults to protect our planet?” said 8-year-old Akeyo. “We are ready to grow food. We are ready to take care of our planet. But we need you to give us opportunities. Don’t just tell us, ’You’re the leaders of tomorrow.’ Let us lead something today. Start with what you have.”
item.source:markdown: At the U.N. climate summit in Antalya, Turkey, Little Miss Environment Kenya 2026, Marren Akeyo, addressed world leaders on their responsibility to take real action to stop climate change. “Climate change does not ask for your birth certificate before affecting you. So, why should we wait until we’re adults to protect our planet?” said 8-year-old Akeyo. “We are ready to grow food. We are ready to take care of our planet. But we need you to give us opportunities. Don’t just tell us, ’You’re the leaders of tomorrow.’ Let us lead something today. Start with what you have.”

item.title: "A COP of Betrayal": U.N. Talks Make No Progress on Fossil Fuel Phaseout, Climate Finance
item.source:markdown:
In our closing broadcast from Antalya, Turkey, the site of the 31st annual U.N. climate change summit, we take a look at what has — and hasn’t — been accomplished at this latest attempt to reach an international framework to stem the impacts of climate change.
“This COP was being touted as a COP of implementation, but what it has become is a COP of betrayal and a COP of distraction,” laments environmental justice advocate Harjeet Singh, the founding director of India’s Satat Sampada Climate Foundation. He’s joined on _Democracy Now!_ by Meena Raman of Friends of the Earth Malaysia and Nafkote Dabi of Oxfam International as a number of NGOs announce their rejection of the conference’s final declaration text, which contains no mentions of fossil fuels or clear financial commitments from polluter countries.
“At the heart of the negotiations right now lies money,” says Dabi. “What rich countries, especially the EU, \[are\] saying is, 'There is no money at home.' But we know there’s money. They can tax the richest. They can tax the excess profit of fossil fuel companies. They can tax private jets. They can tax extreme wealth and raise the funds that’s needed to support communities.”
item.author: webdev@democracynow.org (Democracy Now!)

item.title: "Historic Judgment": World Court Rules Burma Guilty of Genocide Against Rohingya
item.description:
The world’s top court has ruled that Myanmar committed genocide against the country’s Rohingya Muslim minority in a 2017 military crackdown that killed about 10,000 people and drove more than 730,000 refugees into Bangladesh. The landmark ruling is the first time the International Court of Justice has held a nation directly responsible for violating the 1948 Genocide Convention. “This is a vindication of what Rohingyas have been saying for the last almost 50 years, since 1978, when the first wave of genocidal expulsion was conducted by the very same perpetrating institution,” says Burmese dissident scholar Maung Zarni. By recognizing Myanmar’s “identity-based group destruction” of the Royinghas, he says, “the court vindicated [the] Rohingya’s collective articulation, memory and suffering.”

“For the first time in its history, the court has set up a process for restitution and reparation for the members of the Rohingya community,” explains Philippe Sands, an international human rights lawyer who served on the legal team for The Gambia, which first brought the legal case against Myanmar to the ICJ six years ago. Sands discusses next steps for restitution and reparations to Rohingya victims, as well as what the Myanmar judgment means for South Africa’s genocide case against Israel, also before the ICJ.

item.title: U.S. Expands Iranian Blockade As Ship Attacks Continue
item.description: The U.S. expanded its blockade of Iranian ports and coastline to include any ship that receives cargo via ship-to-ship transfer, according to Joint Maritime Information Center. The U.S. reinstated the blockade in July after the memorandum of understanding between Iran and the U.S. failed nearly a month into it. item.source:markdown: The U.S. expanded its blockade of Iranian ports and coastline to include any ship that receives cargo via ship-to-ship transfer, according to Joint Maritime Information Center. Any ship that receives cargo via ship-to-ship transfer from a ship that loaded at an Iranian port or coastline could be considered as attempting to evade the U.S.’s blockade, reads the JMIC advisory. The U.S. reinstated the blockade in July after the memorandum of understanding between Iran and the U.S. failed nearly a month into it. item.title: Russian Indigenous Activist Daria Egereva Remains Jailed; Arrested After 2025 U.N. Climate Talks
item.description:
Human rights and climate groups are calling on Russia to release two prominent activists, Daria Egereva and Natalia Leongardt, who have been held in pretrial detention in Moscow for nearly a year, since December 2025. Egereva, a leading Indigenous rights activist in Russia, was arrested shortly after attending the COP30 United Nations climate summit in Belém, Brazil, where she served as co-chair of the International Indigenous Peoples Forum on Climate Change. Leongardt has worked for decades to support Indigenous rights.

“Right now all we are demanding is the release of Daria and Natalia, because they shouldn’t be in prison. You shouldn’t be arrested for activism,” says Viktor Suliandziga-Bagat, an Indigenous rights activist and representative of the Udege people from the Russian Far East. He is living in exile due to the risk against activists. “I don’t think I can come back to Russia,” he says.

item.title: "Defend the Sacred": Indigenous Activist on Climate & Alaska Native Mary Peltola's Senate Victory
item.description:
Democrat Mary Peltola was declared the winner this week of Alaska’s closely watched race for U.S. Senate, making her the first Alaska Native lawmaker elected to the upper chamber of Congress.

At the COP31 climate conference in Turkey, we speak with Aakaluk Adrienne Blatchford, an Inupiaq and Yup’ik organizer from Unalakleet, Alaska. She says Peltola’s win is a significant milestone for Indigenous peoples in Alaska.

“Having somebody represent us in such a large capacity with such a big weight on her shoulders, but still carrying that struggle with her as she continues to advocate for our people and our way of life, is monumental,” says Blatchford.

item.title: "This Is Not Going Well": COP31 Draft Text Avoids Fossil Fuel Phaseout, Bets on "Magic Technologies"
item.description:
As we continue our week of broadcasts from the global United Nations climate conference known as COP31, we get an update on the formal negotiations from German activist Luisa Neubauer. The latest draft text of the key climate commitments that countries are debating has dropped language about phasing out fossil fuels, but it does include an emphasis on carbon capture and storage — a largely unproven technology that critics say cannot be deployed at scale to curb emissions.

“We have much better solutions at hand, like renewables,” says Neubauer. “This is not going well. We are not doing fine. And if anything, after this conference ends, we need people to take the streets and fight for more justice out there.”
item.source:markdown:
As we continue our week of broadcasts from the global United Nations climate conference known as COP31, we get an update on the formal negotiations from German activist Luisa Neubauer. The [latest draft text](https://unfccc.int/documents/665726) of the key climate commitments that countries are debating has dropped language about phasing out fossil fuels, but it does include an emphasis on carbon capture and storage — a largely unproven technology that critics say cannot be deployed at scale to curb emissions.
“We have much better solutions at hand, like renewables,” says Neubauer. “This is not going well. We are not doing fine. And if anything, after this conference ends, we need people to take the streets and fight for more justice out there.”

item.title: A New International Order? Xi, Trump & Putin Hold Historic Trilateral Summit in China
item.source:markdown:
Chinese President Xi Jinping hosted his U.S. and Russian counterparts for a historic trilateral summit on Thursday, with the leaders of the three biggest nuclear superpowers meeting for about 90 minutes in Shenzhen. Afterward, the countries published a “peace declaration” that affirmed “nuclear war cannot be won and must never be fought.” The declaration also announced a commitment to increase petroleum production, called for reforms at the United Nations and urged the International Criminal Court and similar bodies to “not abuse their jurisdiction.”
While in China, President Donald Trump also had a separate meeting with President Vladimir Putin to discuss the war in Ukraine, though it’s unclear if they made any progress.
“It’s a significant post-1945 moment, which was the last time that we had great summits,” says Scott Lucas, professor of international politics at University College Dublin. “What is the most important takeaway … is an ascendant China. It was China that really set the terms of what was said.”

item.title: New grad rules for Alberta high schools have people talking
item.description: Trading English for phys ed? Alberta's government says students entering high school in 2028 will only need 47 credits in core classes, down from the current 56. The government's new requirements mean that students will only need to complete one senior level course in either English or social studies, while senior level math and science classes will still be optional. What will be mandatory though is physical education.
item.source:markdown:

item.title: Ecuador Pushes to Expand Amazon Oil Drilling While Land Defenders Face Threats
item.description: Ecuadorians voted overwhelmingly in 2023 to stop oil extraction at Yasuní National Park, one of the most biodiverse places on Earth, yet oil drilling has continued despite that historic referendum. “The government does not want to close the wells,” says Ivonne Yánez, the president of Acción Ecológica, an environmental nonprofit group based in Ecuador. The Ecuadorian government is also “continuing expanding the oil activities in the Amazon,” she points out. Yánez also speaks about how dangerous Latin America is for environmental activists. It is where “the most number of defenders that are just defending their lands, their rivers, their rights,” are killed. “And in Ecuador, this is also happening.”

item.title: "Shameful": Fossil Fuel Industry Blocks U.N. Climate Action as Global Warming Reaches 1.5°C
item.description: As Democracy Now! continues broadcasting from the U.N. climate summit in Antalya, Turkey, we speak with Rachel Cleetus, climate program director at the Union of Concerned Scientists, about climate finance — the notion that efforts to mitigate the climate crisis must be funded. “Climate finance is not an abstract thing. It’s what countries need to be able to transition away from fossil fuels,” says Cleetus. “And right now we have pennies in these funds.” She notes that at a pledging event for the Adaptation Fund, which supports climate finance for developing countries, a mere $50 million was pledged. “It’s shameful, absolutely unjust, what’s happening here. And richer countries are continuing to block progress.” This comes as scientists say the world is set to overshoot the target, set by the 2015 Paris Agreement, of limiting global heating to 1.5 degrees Celsius.

item.title: "Ecocide": Colombia's New Right-Wing Gov't Ends Amazon Protections, Rejects Fossil Fuel Phaseout
item.source:markdown:
The U.N. climate summit comes seven months after a major climate meeting was held in Santa Marta, Colombia, where more than 50 countries gathered for a groundbreaking effort to push for phasing out fossil fuels to combat the climate crisis. The initiative was championed by Colombian President Gustavo Petro, whose term ended in August, but Colombia’s new right-wing President Abelardo de la Espriella has withdrawn Colombia from the Santa Marta coalition.
“Colombia has just reversed the protection of the Amazon,” says Irene Vélez-Torres, former Colombian environment minister under Petro. “What we are seeing is really an ecocide taking place in Colombia.”
Meanwhile, at COP31, “there are petro lobbyists, people here defending the interest of the corporations, and therefore the discussions cannot make any progress,” Vélez-Torres adds. “The agreements cannot even mention the word 'fossil fuels.'”
item.author: webdev@democracynow.org (Democracy Now!)

item.title: Voices from Turkey: "The More Oppressive the Regime Gets, the More Resilient People Become"
item.description:
As climate negotiations enter their crucial final stretch in the last few days of COP31, held in Antalya, Turkey, dozens of human rights groups urged Turkish authorities to release four LGBTQ+ activists ahead of a hearing that has just begun at a court in Istanbul. Back in September, Turkish authorities began a large-scale crackdown on LGBTQ+ organizations and activists, raiding offices, blocking social media accounts and websites, arresting at least 116 people and launching criminal investigations into at least 160 people. Meanwhile, since last month, Turkey’s last two remaining opposition television channels have been brought under government control. This follows the Turkish government’s widespread crackdown on the main opposition party with dozens of mayors arrested since 2024.

Despite Turkey’s authoritarianism, in Antalya, many of the Turkish groups critical of the government gathered in large numbers at the People’s Climate Summit, an alternative gathering to the U.N. climate summit organized by a coalition of Turkish environmental groups. For more, we hear from a number of activists from across Turkish civil society, including Berkan Özyer, the director of Greenpeace Türkiye, who tells us that “the more oppressive [a] regime gets, the more resilient people become.”

As climate negotiations enter their crucial final stretch in the last few days of COP31, held in Antalya, Turkey, dozens of human rights groups urged Turkish authorities to release four LGBTQ+ activists ahead of a hearing that has just begun at a court in Istanbul. Back in September, Turkish authorities began a large-scale crackdown on LGBTQ+ organizations and activists, raiding offices, blocking social media accounts and websites, arresting at least 116 people and launching criminal investigations into at least 160 people. Meanwhile, since last month, Turkey’s last two remaining opposition television channels have been brought under government control. This follows the Turkish government’s widespread crackdown on the main opposition party with dozens of mayors arrested since 2024.
Despite Turkey’s authoritarianism, in Antalya, many of the Turkish groups critical of the government gathered in large numbers at the People’s Climate Summit, an alternative gathering to the U.N. climate summit organized by a coalition of Turkish environmental groups. For more, we hear from a number of activists from across Turkish civil society, including Berkan Özyer, the director of Greenpeace Türkiye, who tells us that “the more oppressive \[a\] regime gets, the more resilient people become.”

item.title: Suspected Russian Aircraft Violated Japan’s Airspace, Says Defense Minister
item.description: Suspected Russian aircraft violated Japanese territorial airspace twice on Thursdays, prompting fighter aircraft to be scrambled in response, Japan’s Defense Minister announced Tuesday. Between 4:07 and 4:10 a.m. on Thursday, one suspected Russian aircraft violated Japanese airspace northwest of Okinoshima, which lies in the East China Sea, Defense Minister Shinjiro Koizumi said in his regularly scheduled Tuesday press conference. Subsequently, between 4:09 and 4:12 a.m., a second suspected Russian aircraft violated Japanese airspace in the same area. The aircraft passed through the Tsushima Strait, flew between Yonaguni Island and Taiwan, and proceeded into the Philippine Sea. Japan Air Self-Defense Force

item.title: As U.S. Boycotts U.N. Climate Talks, California Leads State/City Efforts to Combat Climate Crisis
item.description:
For the second year in a row, the Trump administration has not sent an official delegation to the United Nations’ annual climate change conference, held this year in Antalya, Turkey. But although no federal representatives are present, more than 120 U.S. state and local leaders are participating, including the governor of the fourth-largest economy in the world, California Governor Gavin Newsom. Newsom, a likely candidate for the 2028 Democratic presidential nomination, has endorsed the Santa Marta Process, a coalition of nations working to develop a global green energy transition.

“The petrostates have made it abundantly clear: Under the current rules of consensus, they are never, ever going to allow COPs to succeed. They’re just not going to sign that agreement. So, essentially, the Santa Marta coalition is making an end run around that, using economic power,” says longtime environmental and climate reporter Mark Hertsgaard.

item.title: Fossil Fuels Are "Undermining Democracy" & Must Be Phased Out: Climate Activist Kumi Naidoo at COP31
item.description: What will it take to bring an end to the fossil fuel era? We speak to Kumi Naidoo, the president of the Fossil Fuel Treaty Initiative, which aims to reach a binding agreement for a global transition away from fossil fuels. Currently backed by over 25 countries from the Global South, the intergovernmental process began earlier this year in Santa Marta, Colombia. Meanwhile, at the United Nations, “for 30 years of negotiations, we don’t have any mention of fossil fuels [in the outcome document]. That’s like Alcoholics Anonymous holding 30 years of conferences and not mentioning alcohol,” says Naidoo. We discuss the Fossil Fuel Treaty Initiative’s goals, how the oil and gas industry drives global conflict, and the Trump administration’s glaring absence from international action on climate change.

item.title: COP31: The push to protect warming oceans reaches the negotiating table
item.description: From identifying marine life with a cup of seawater to drawing on Indigenous knowledge to prevent wildfires, scientists and communities showcased both cutting-edge and time-tested ways to protect nature at COP31 on Tuesday. Yet turning innovation into action remains a challenge, with funding gaps persisting and ministers struggling to bridge divisions over fossil fuels and climate finance as negotiations enter their final days.
item.source:markdown: From identifying marine life with a cup of seawater to drawing on Indigenous knowledge to prevent wildfires, scientists and communities showcased both cutting-edge and time-tested ways to protect nature at COP31 on Tuesday. item.title: USS Theodore Roosevelt Now in the Middle East, Lincoln’s Last Escorts Finally Home
item.description: A third U.S. aircraft carrier and its escorts are now in the Middle East. USS Theodore Roosevelt (CVN-71) chopped into U.S. 5th Fleet on Sunday. The arrival of the Theodore Roosevelt Carrier Strike Group makes three U.S. carrier strike groups in the Middle East, as tensions persist between the U.S. and Iran. Over the weekend, the Houthis continued to claim areas around the Bab el-Mandeb – the strategic chokepoint that connects the Gulf of Aden to the Red Sea – while Iranian forces claim they attacked a U.S. radar in Bahrain on Friday. U.S. Central Command denied the claim posting

item.title: "Coffers Are Never Empty…For Bombs": Climate Activist Asad Rehman on Need for Climate Finance
item.description:
The United Nations climate summit in Antalya, Turkey, is in its second and final week. To get an update on the state of negotiations among countries, we speak with longtime climate campaigner Asad Rehman, the chief executive of Friends of the Earth England, Wales and Northern Ireland. He says rich, developed countries are still dragging their feet on a rapid transition away from fossil fuels while withholding the money that poorer, Global South countries need.

“Whether you’re cutting emissions, whether you’re adapting to the impacts of climate change or dealing with incredible losses which are totalling over a trillion right now, you need public finance,” says Rehman. “And the rich countries are saying, 'Our coffers are empty.' But, of course, the coffers are never empty when it comes to paying for bombs. It’s never empty when it comes to the fossil fuel subsidies to the corporate giants, and it’s never empty when it comes to the billionaires.”

item.title: Global Warming Approaches 1.5 Degrees in "Calamity for the World's Ecosystems"
item.description:
As delegates, industry lobbyists and civil society activists attend this year’s United Nations climate summit, known as COP31, we speak with international environmental lawyer Farhana Yamin about the state of global climate efforts. Yamin helped write the landmark 2015 Paris Agreement and has attended 28 of the last 31 U.N. climate summits. The Paris Agreement aimed to keep global temperatures below 1.5 degrees Celsius above preindustrial levels, a threshold that climate scientists say the world will now overshoot.

“It’s a moment of great sadness, actually, for the world community that we weren’t able to start the phaseout, start the acceleration of the transition away from fossil fuels 10 years earlier,” says Yamin. “So, we’re about 10 years behind, but I hope that over time that we can accelerate.”

item.title: People's Climate March: Thousands Demonstrate in Turkey as Country Hosts COP31 U.N. Summit
item.description:
Democracy Now! is in Antalya, Turkey, where this year’s United Nations climate summit, COP31, is being held. For the second year in a row, the United States has not sent an official delegation to the international talks, in keeping with the Trump administration’s longstanding hostility to such efforts to address the climate crisis.

There are nearly 100,000 participants here at this year’s climate summit, including many civil society activists from Turkey and around the globe. Over the weekend, Democracy Now! was in the streets of Antalya to speak with some of the thousands of protesters who marched to demand urgent climate action, including many labor leaders.

“Trade unions care about a lot more than just protecting jobs. We have systemic demands,” said Lala Peñaranda, the Latin America coordinator for Trade Unions for Energy Democracy.

item.title: Do Quebec police recruits get enough racial profiling training? We checked the curriculum
item.description: At Quebec's provincial police academy, aspiring officers spend hundreds of hours on technical skills crucial to the job, from firing weapons to physically restraining suspects. Far less of their time explicitly addresses issues such as racial profiling and ethical breaches — which led to the firing of seven Montreal police officers earlier this month.
item.source:markdown:

item.title: Peacoat Evicted from Navy Seabags After a Century at Sea
item.description: The traditional Navy peacoat will be no more. A new Navy uniform policy released on Friday removes the peacoat, acrylic V-neck sweater and dinner dress white jacket from a sailor’s seabag beginning on Oct. 1, 2027. Sailors may still wear the wool V-neck sweater. Instead of the dinner dress white jacket, sailors will now use the dinner dress blue jacket as the standard formal uniform year-round, according to the policy. item.title: The Rule of Law Project: New Effort Launched to Probe Corruption & State Violence in U.S.
item.description:
As Democrats prepare to take control of Congress in January, party leaders say they intend to hold Trump officials accountable with stepped-up hearings and investigations. The administration, however, has responded with threats to launch its own investigations into lawmakers for carrying out their oversight responsibilities.

“The oversight function of Congress is well established by the founders. It’s a normal part of government. The separation of powers requires oversight,” says Brad Adams, co-founder of The Rule of Law Project, which seeks to provide outside accountability due to what he describes as the administration’s refusal to investigate “obvious cases of corruption.”

item.title: "It's Just Barbarism": Dr. Feroze Sidhwa Mourns Friend Killed in Israeli Hospital Strike in Gaza
item.description:
Israel’s latest bombing of Nasser Hospital in Gaza on Thursday killed six Palestinians, including surgeon Dr. Rizk Abu Shaira. He was featured in the recent documentary American Doctor, which follows international medical volunteers in Gaza’s battered hospitals as they work alongside Palestinian colleagues.

Israel claimed, without providing evidence, that it targeted a senior Hamas militant in the hospital strike. Israel has repeatedly bombed medical facilities in Gaza since the start of the genocide in October 2023, even though such attacks are prohibited under international law.

“It’s just barbarism. I don’t know why we’re supporting this,” says Dr. Feroze Sidhwa, one of the titular American doctors in the documentary, who demands accountability for Israel’s actions and a change in U.S. policy toward the country. “That’s an American-made bomb dropped by an American-made airplane burning American-supplied jet fuel.”

Sidhwa also comments on the catastrophic flooding in Gaza that has swamped the temporary shelters of tens of thousands of displaced Palestinians as Israel continues to block the entry of shelter materials into the territory. As a result, “babies are going to die of hypothermia in Gaza for the fourth year in a row,” Sidhwa says.

item.title: "Parasitic Technology": Could Jensen Huang/Nvidia Scandal Prompt Rethink About AI?
item.description:
Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang resigned Thursday after reports of multiple extramarital affairs, including with an employee and a Chinese businesswoman whom U.S. intelligence officials accuse of spying for Beijing. The company says Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress will serve as interim CEO as the board searches for a permanent replacement.

Nvidia’s computer chips are at the heart of the artificial intelligence boom, driving the company’s value above $4 trillion and making Huang one of the most influential business leaders in the world. His spectacular fall from the company he co-founded in 1993 comes as the U.S. stock market has become highly dependent on a handful of AI-related companies and amid intense competition between the United States and China over control of the technology, with access to Nvidia’s chips becoming a major point of contention between the two countries.

Tech critic Paris Marx notes that the AI industry’s “circular financing,” in which companies are both clients and investors for one another, has created systemic risk.

We also speak with Ramesh Srinivasan, director of the AI Futures Lab at UCLA, who says the “soap opera” of the Huang scandal has exposed “how precarious the governance of this AI truly is,” with only a handful of people and firms controlling “incredibly powerful technology that feeds off of all of us and the planet.”

item.title: Security Council LIVE: Fragile Gulf calm tested as threats to Hormuz shipping mount
item.description: Nearly nine months after Israeli and US strikes on Iran set off a regional war, the Gulf remains on a knife edge. Iran has all but closed the Strait of Hormuz, which carried a fifth of the world’s oil before the conflict. Attacks on shipping are rising, and efforts to stop a return to full-scale fighting have yet to produce a deal. The Security Council is meeting at Bahrain’s request to discuss the threat to regional and maritime security. Follow live below – and for full meetings coverage year round, go here.

item.title: COP31: Climate finance falls short as calls grow for polluters to pay
item.description: From emotional appeals for climate justice to high-stakes negotiations over billions of dollars, finance dominated discussions at COP31 on Friday. item.source:markdown: From emotional appeals for climate justice to high-stakes negotiations over billions of dollars, finance dominated discussions at COP31 on Friday. item.title: From Ranked-Choice Voting to Dumping Electoral College: Rob Richie on Election Reform Movement
item.source:markdown:
Alaska is the only Senate race yet to be called. Democratic challenger Mary Peltola is narrowly leading Republican incumbent Dan Sullivan with about 86% of votes counted. Alaska uses ranked-choice voting, a system where voters choose not only their top candidate, but can also indicate an order of preference for remaining candidates on the ballot. If no candidate wins a majority as the top choice, then second-choice votes are added to the totals and so on until there is a winner.
Rob Richie, president and founder of Expand Democracy and a senior adviser with FairVote, explains how ranked-choice voting has shaped the Alaska race and how it is “a system that promotes \[candidates\] reaching out, engaging, and, for voters, a lot of freedom.”
Richie adds that Peltola is “heavily favored to win at this point.”

item.title: "Don't F#*k It Up, Democrats": David Sirota on Direction of Party & Fight Over Jeffries & Schumer
item.description:
With Democrats set to take control of both chambers of Congress in January, Vermont Senator Bernie Sanders says he will not support Chuck Schumer for another term as the Democratic Senate leader, calling for the party to move in “a new and bold direction.” Michigan Democratic Senator Elissa Slotkin has said she will not support Schumer unless he presents a plan to govern differently, and several senators-elect have called for new leadership or declined to endorse Schumer. Maryland Senator Chris Van Hollen is considering challenging Schumer. Meanwhile, Hakeem Jeffries is facing questions about his leadership of House Democrats after 11 of the party’s members missed a key vote on impeaching Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth.

After “a big win for the populist wing of the Democratic Party, … it would be a betrayal for that election to result immediately in the Democratic Party simply responding by reelecting the same leadership,” says David Sirota, editor-in-chief of The Lever.

item.title: Relatives of Slain Freedom Summer Activists Celebrate Scott Colom's Historic Senate Win in Mississippi
item.source:markdown:
Democrat Scott Colom has defeated incumbent Cindy Hyde-Smith to become Mississippi’s first African American senator since the post-Civil War Reconstruction era. The electoral breakthrough is particularly meaningful given Mississippi’s history in the civil rights movement. In 1964, three civil rights activists — James Chaney, Michael Schwerner and Andrew Goodman — were murdered by the Ku Klux Klan after traveling to the state to register Black voters. We speak with two of their relatives about Colom’s stunning upset.
“I believe that people were voting for help. And they evidently saw something in Mr. Colom that made them feel like that they could hope again and that he was the help that was needed,” says Angela Lewis, the daughter of James Chaney.
“The people of Mississippi have spoken,” adds David Goodman, the brother of Andrew Goodman. “And we have to cease and desist this divide-and-conquer business, because it’s not in our collective interest as the United States of America.”

item.title: Scott Colom Wins Stunning Victory, Becomes Mississippi's First Black Senator Since Reconstruction
item.description:
Democrat Scott Colom has made history as Mississippi’s first Democratic senator since 1982 — and its first African American senator since the post-Civil War Reconstruction era. Colom narrowly defeated Republican incumbent Senator Cindy Hyde-Smith in a state that President Trump won by nearly 23 points in 2024. Colom’s victory brings the incoming Senate Democratic caucus to 55. Colom gave his victory speech on Wednesday at the historically Black Tougaloo College, just miles from where civil rights activist Medgar Evers was murdered in 1963 by a member of the Ku Klux Klan.

“There were times that I couldn’t get donors to answer the phone; they did not believe a moment like this was possible. But I kept the faith,” said Colom. “There are so many people that had faith in Mississippi at times where it seemed impossible, people like Medgar Evers.”

item.title: "Birds of War": New Film Tells a Story of Love and Journalism from Syria to Lebanon
item.description:
We speak with Janay Boulos and Abd Alkader Habak, filmmakers and subjects of the new documentary Birds of War, which tells their epic love story through years of upheaval in the Middle East. Boulos, a London-based Lebanese journalist working for the BBC, and Habak, a Syrian activist and cameraman, first connected while covering the Syrian civil war and stayed in touch through years of war, revolution and exile, forming a relationship that is chronicled in the documentary by drawing on 13 years of their personal videos, voice notes and other correspondence.

The film also examines the unequal relationship between international news organizations and local journalists whose work they rely on, the fraught political history between Syria and Lebanon, and how Boulos and Habak’s personal connection overcame those divisions.

“Without our journalistic relationship, [we] would have never been together. I would have never opened my heart to somebody like him,” says Boulos. “We can be any race, any gender, any religion, any background, but at the same time we’re all humans.”

Birds of War premiered at the 2026 Sundance Film Festival, where it won the World Cinema Documentary Special Jury Award for Journalistic Impact.

item.title: Meet David Morales: Providence Voters Elect Democratic Socialist Mayor, Approve Israel Divestment
item.description:
Voters in Providence, Rhode Island, approved a ballot measure last week that could result in the city divesting from Israel. The successful grassroots campaign makes Providence the first U.S. city to pass a binding divestment measure through a popular vote. The measure instructs the city to divest from countries and companies implicated in “ethnic cleansing, apartheid, illegal military occupation, or genocide.” The language does not mention Israel by name. We speak with one of the key backers of the divestment measure, Mayor-elect David Morales, a 28-year-old democratic socialist who made history on election night as the youngest mayor ever elected in Providence.

“What we saw was our neighbors coming out in the thousands to demonstrate that we are ready for change,” Morales says, promising to enact his affordability-focused platform. “It’s the responsibility of local government to take action. And for that reason, we are seeing a rise in democratic socialism and the representation of democratic socialists all across the country.”
item.source:markdown:
Voters in Providence, Rhode Island, approved a ballot measure last week that could result in the city divesting from Israel. The successful grassroots campaign makes Providence the first U.S. city to pass a binding divestment measure through a popular vote. The measure instructs the city to divest from countries and companies implicated in “ethnic cleansing, apartheid, illegal military occupation, or genocide.” The language does not mention Israel by name. We speak with one of the key backers of the divestment measure, Mayor-elect David Morales, a 28-year-old democratic socialist who made history on election night as the youngest mayor ever elected in Providence.
“What we saw was our neighbors coming out in the thousands to demonstrate that we are ready for change,” Morales says, promising to enact his affordability-focused platform. “It’s the responsibility of local government to take action. And for that reason, we are seeing a rise in democratic socialism and the representation of democratic socialists all across the country.”

item.title: "American Scoundrel": From Roy Cohn to Stephen Miller, "McCarthyism Lives On," Says Author Kai Bird
item.description:
We speak with historian Kai Bird about American Scoundrel, a new biography of the notorious political fixer Roy Cohn, who rose to fame as chief counsel to Joe McCarthy during the senator’s anti-communist campaign, served as a lawyer for the New York mob, and was an influential voice in Republican circles until his death from AIDS-related complications in 1986. His most impactful relationship, however, would prove to be with a young Donald Trump, whom he mentored in business and politics during the 1970s and ’80s.

Facing political setbacks during his first term as president, Trump reportedly asked, “Where’s my Roy Cohn?” Bird, who co-authored American Scoundrel with his wife Susan Goldmark, says Trump may have found his Cohn in Stephen Miller, the architect of the administration’s mass deportation policies whom Trump just elevated to chief of staff.

“It’s not really a surprise that, cornered and wounded by the recent election results, he reaches out and pulls up Stephen Miller, who’s very similar in his willingness to go on the offensive and never back down, and to say outrageous things to try to change the narrative,” says Bird.
item.source:markdown:

item.title: Canadians fought a war in Afghanistan. Why do we struggle to talk about it?
item.description: Is Afghanistan in danger of becoming Canada's forgotten war? Parliament is struggling with a bill that would designate the 13-year conflict — where more than 40,000 Canadians served — as a war. The prime minister's Veterans' Week statement mentions the tragedy in Wainwright and service in the first Gulf War, but not Afghanistan. And an increasing number of veterans say the war and understanding what happened is now slipping from the national conscience.

item.title: Meet Will Lawrence: Sunrise Movement Co-Founder Elected to Congress on Anti-Data Center Platform
item.description:
Progressive candidate Will Lawrence of Michigan has defeated Republican incumbent Tom Barrett, flipping the state’s 7th Congressional District, a closely watched swing district that includes Lansing. Lawrence, the co-founder of the youth-led climate organization Sunrise Movement, refused corporate PAC money, instead building a people-powered grassroots mobilization campaign. He focused on lowering the costs of housing and healthcare, opposing the war on Iran, and challenging the power of Big Tech.

“I’m fighting for a federal moratorium on new data center development, along with a pause on advanced AI development,” says Lawrence. “These developers come into small towns, and they say, ’We’re going to suck up a bunch of water. We’re going to use more energy than the current capacity of the grid. We don’t know what’s going to happen to your property values, but if everything goes well, we’re going to put 10 or 20 million people out of work, and if it goes poorly, we may kill everybody by accident.’”

Lawrence also says he will back Hakeem Jeffries for House speaker, but that he will demand Democratic leadership listen to progressive concerns.

item.title: "We Have to Be Brave": Palestinian Journalist Abed Abu Shehadeh Speaks Out After Israeli Detention
item.description:
The prominent journalist Abed Abu Shehadeh, a Palestinian citizen of Israel, has been released from Israeli custody after five days in detention. He was arrested on Wednesday by armed police and Shin Bet agents who conducted a nighttime raid on his home in the Israeli city of Jaffa. Abu Shehadeh’s detention was related to his reporting on the October 27 Israeli election and the role of Palestinian political parties. Ahead of the election, he interviewed Azmi Bishara, a Palestinian intellectual and former member of the Israeli Knesset who has lived in exile in Qatar since fleeing Israel amid allegations that he aided Hezbollah during the 2006 Lebanon war. Israeli authorities detained Abu Shehadeh on suspicion of “contacting a foreign agent,” in connection to his interview with Bishara.

“Men with ski masks knock on your door at 11 at night. They tell you that they have an arrest warrant. They raid the house. They wake your wife, your children,” says Shehadeh. “It tells how messianic and dangerous the extreme right in Israel has become, willing to use this unprecedented power against journalists.”

item.title: Pentagon Whistleblower Wes Bryant: Impeach Hegseth. He's a "Clear & Present Danger" to Democracy
item.description:
The House of Representatives is moving toward a vote this week on whether to impeach Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth. Outgoing Republican Congressmember Thomas Massie of Kentucky introduced eight articles of impeachment against Hegseth on Monday. They include violating the 1973 War Powers Resolution by continuing to attack Iran after Congress ordered the Trump administration to stop, illegally waging war against Yemen, ignoring laws designed to reduce civilian casualties, overseeing “extrajudicial killings” by bombing the boats of alleged drug traffickers in the Caribbean and eastern Pacific, abducting President Nicolás Maduro of Venezuela without congressional authorization, and suppressing the free speech rights of Democratic Senator Mark Kelly in retaliation for his participation in a video reminding troops not to obey illegal orders. If the House votes for impeachment, it will prompt a Senate trial that could end with removal from office.

“Under Hegseth, the U.S. military has been hijacked,” says retired Air Force Master Sergeant Wes Bryant, who served as chief of civilian harm assessment at the Pentagon from 2024 to 2025. “America has portrayed itself to the world as a far-right dictatorship bent on global domination, and Hegseth and his wielding of the U.S. military with free rein from Donald Trump is really the primary enforcer of that.”

Bryant adds that “Hegseth should be the first domino,” but that Trump, as well as “many of our senior military leaders,” should also be impeached.

item.title: SS United States Towed from Mobile Berth Ahead of Sinking
item.description: The hulk of the ocean liner and secret troop transport SS United States was towed from its berth in Mobile, Ala., ahead of its sinking to become an artificial reef off the coast of Florida, according to ship spotters. Bought in 2024 by Okaloosa County, Fla., from a group that had failed to turn the ship into a floating museum, SS United States has been moored in Mobile since March of 2025 undergoing the final preparations before being sunk. The work included removing items from the ship, cleaning tanks and the smokestacks for a planned installation ashore. A judge denied

item.title: Hegseth Calls for Sweeping Military Education Changes in Naval War College Address
item.description: Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth announced sweeping education directives supporting his effort to de-civilianize military higher education and align it with warfighting priorities on Monday at the Naval War College. A total of 33 directives were unveiled on Monday. Among key changes were an AI-aided capstone wargame in lieu of a written thesis for graduates and expanded access to classified information for course instruction. To facilitate greater use of classified information in the study of war, Hegseth said he was ordering accelerated capital investments to build and expand sensitive compartmented information facilities or SCIFs, at every war college campus to clear

item.title: Could Nvidia survive without its ultra-powerful CEO, Jensen Huang?
item.description: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has helmed the company since starting it in 1993, guiding it from a graphics card maker to the AI behemoth it is today. But with an investigation now underway into whether Huang was the target of a foreign intelligence effort and no clear successor in sight, analysts say a change at the top — if it were deemed necessary — would be massive.

Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has helmed the company since starting it in 1993, guiding it from a graphics card maker to the AI behemoth it is today. item.title: Royal Navy Commissions First Unmanned Surface Vehicle Squadron
item.description: The Royal Navy commissioned its first unmanned surface vessel squadron last week as it transforms into a hybrid fleet, the service announced Monday. The 1st Autonomous Squadron was formally commissioned in a ceremony on Thursday at His Majesty’s Naval Base, in Portsmouth, England, according to a news release. The unit is the Royal Navy’s first ever autonomous squadron. “That makes this a genuinely historic occasion. For generations, the fleet has been built around ships, submarines and aircraft, manned by sailors and Royal Marines. From today, an autonomous squadron takes its place alongside them,” Royal Navy Fleet Commander Vice Adm. Steve

item.title: "A Crackdown on All Independent Voices": Egypt Shutters News Outlets, Prosecutes Editor Lina Attalah
item.description:
Lina Attalah, editor-in-chief of Egypt’s leading independent news outlet Mada Masr, faces a criminal trial this week on charges of “spreading false information,” just two weeks after being convicted of operating an unlicensed website and fined more than $50,000. A judge also ordered the publication to be shut down. The cases are part of a broader crackdown on independent Egyptian media under the government of President Abdel Fattah el-Sisi, including the arrest of the entire newsroom of another outlet, Matsadaash. More than 100 organizations, including Amnesty International, Human Rights Watch and the Committee to Protect Journalists, have condemned the arrests and prosecutions and called on Egyptian authorities to drop the charges.

“Putting us in jail is not going to solve the country’s problems,” Attalah told Democracy Now! in an interview Friday. “We need to be operating as journalists in our newsrooms as opposed to being defendants in courtrooms.”

Attalah says she and Mada Masr will appeal the ruling to shut them down, hoping to “use this crisis” as a way to fight censorship in Egypt and expand the space for independent reporting.
item.source:markdown:
Lina Attalah, editor-in-chief of Egypt’s leading independent news outlet _Mada Masr_, faces a criminal trial this week on charges of “spreading false information,” just two weeks after being convicted of operating an unlicensed website and fined more than $50,000. A judge also ordered the publication to be shut down. The cases are part of a broader crackdown on independent Egyptian media under the government of President Abdel Fattah el-Sisi, including the arrest of the entire newsroom of another outlet, _Matsadaash_. More than 100 organizations, including Amnesty International, Human Rights Watch and the Committee to Protect Journalists, have condemned the arrests and prosecutions and called on Egyptian authorities to drop the charges.
“Putting us in jail is not going to solve the country’s problems,” Attalah told _Democracy Now!_ in an interview Friday. “We need to be operating as journalists in our newsrooms as opposed to being defendants in courtrooms.”
Attalah says she and _Mada Masr_ will appeal the ruling to shut them down, hoping to “use this crisis” as a way to fight censorship in Egypt and expand the space for independent reporting.
